It can perform the following tasks (Special licenses may be needed):. • Static analysis of load cases acting upon three-dimensional structures, as well as planar and axisymmetric structures.. • Static analysis of load cases after second-order theory. • Computation of the natural frequencies of three-dimensional structures..
 • Computation of the buckling eigenvalues of three-dimensional structures.

 Implicit direct integration of the equations of motion for structures with arbitrary damping

 The static system is stored in the database after its generation e.g. by the program SOFiMSHA, SOFiMSHC or SOFiPLUS.
 The following elements can be processed by DYNA:
 • Point masses (with off diagonal components)
 • Three-dimensional prismatic bending beams with haunches, warping torsion and bedding profiles (piles)
 • Truss- and cable elements
 • Spring elements, boundary and FLEX elements
 • Scaled boundary finite elements (SBFEM)
 • Damping elements
 • Shell elements
 3D-solid elements
 For the explicit integration not all features are supported. Only the truss, cable, spring and the 3D volume (BRIC) element are available. All interactions (Wind, Loadtrain, Soil) are not available. But geometric and material nonlinearity are supported.
 The results of the dynamic analysis including the mode shapes are stored in the database as displacements and stresses with a load case number.
 The mode shapes can also be transferred from the database after a calculation with the pro- gram ASE.
 For the purposes of a dynamic analysis, the program may output the maximal and the minimal of all displacements, velocities or accelerations as well as internal forces and moments, and eventually the time variation of selected degrees of freedom or internal forces and moments.
 For speed reasons almost all algorithms follow what is called IN-CORE solutions. The size of the problem is therefore limited by the amount of available main memory. Modal solutions transferring the eigenvalues from ASE are not subjected to this limitations.

- Above the block, slightly to its left, is a horizontal arrow pointing to the right, labeled “u(t).” This indicates the displacement of the mass as a function of time.  
- To the right of the mass block, at mid‐height, is a bold horizontal arrow pointing outward, labeled “p(t).” This represents the external excitation force applied to the mass.  

2. Right‐hand side: Free‐body force depiction  
- Separated by a gap, the mass block is sketched again on the far right, unshaded. No wall or connections are shown on this side—only the block outline.  
- Two horizontal arrows, both originating at the block’s right face and pointing back toward the block’s center (i.e., to the left), are drawn.

3. Caption

Overall, this figure illustrates a single‐degree‐of‐freedom linear dynamic system comprised of an inertial mass m, a linear spring of stiffness k, and a viscous damper with damping coefficient c. The left assembly shows how the spring, damper, and external force p(t) connect to the mobile mass, while the right sketch clarifies the internal restoring forces—k·u(t) and c·u̇(t)—acting opposite to the positive displacement direction u(t). This visual supports the derivation of the standard equation of motion m·ü(t) + c·u̇(t) + k·u(t) = p(t).

 (2.1)
 where (t), ˙(t) and ¨(t) are displacement, velocity and acceleration, while k, c and m are stiffness, damping and mass of the SDOF system, respectively. p(t) is the external excitation force.

1. Acceleration ü(τ)

   • Right (linear‐acceleration):

     – Graph: a sloping dashed line rising from ü_i at τ=0 to ü_{i+1} at τ=Δt.

2. Velocity u̇(τ)

“Figure 2.2: Average acceleration (left) and linear acceleration (right) methods.”

Visually, the left column emphasizes simplicity—constant acceleration yields straight‐line velocity and parabolic displacement—while the right column shows how allowing acceleration to vary linearly within the step produces curved velocity profiles and a cubic component in displacement. This comparison underpins choices in time‐integration schemes (e.g., the Newmark family), where trade‐offs between algorithmic complexity, accuracy, and numerical damping are governed by how one interpolates acceleration over Δt.

Linear interpolation  
• A dotted (or dashed) straight line connects the top of the bar at tᵢ to the top of the bar at tᵢ₊₁, indicating the assumption of constant variation of acceleration over Δt.  

Intermediate sampling points  
• A thin vertical dotted line at tᵢ + (1 – α) Δt indicates the evaluation point used in the α‐method: the time within the interval where the equilibrium equation is enforced to introduce numerical damping without degrading accuracy.  
• A second vertical dotted line farther to the right at tᵢ + θ Δt extends beyond tᵢ₊₁ by (θ – 1) Δt, showing the “overshoot” sampling time used in the Wilson-θ method to enhance stability by evaluating equilibrium at a future instant.  

Time-step annotation  
• Beneath the horizontal axis, a double-headed arrow spans from tᵢ to tᵢ₊₁ and is labeled “Δt,” denoting the basic integration interval.  

Caption  
At the bottom, the figure is labeled “Figure 2.3: Integration in time – α and Wilson-θ methods.”  

Overall, the graphic clearly locates the start and end accelerations, depicts their linear interpolation, and highlights the two key internal and extrapolated sample times (tᵢ + (1 – α) Δt and tᵢ + θ Δt) that distinguish the α‐method and the Wilson-θ method in time-integration schemes.

The figure consists of two related plots, (a) and (b), each showing how a single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) damped system responds to a steady harmonic excitation as a function of the frequency ratio η = ωp∕ω (excitation frequency divided by the undamped natural frequency).

1. General Layout  
 • Both plots share the same horizontal axis, labeled η = ωp∕ω, running from 0 to 4.  
 • A vertical dashed line at η = 1 highlights the resonance condition (excitation frequency equal to natural frequency).  
 • Horizontal dashed reference lines appear in each plot:  
   – In (a) at RD = 1, indicating unity magnification (static response level).  
   – In (b) at φ = 90° and φ = 180°, marking the phase-lag benchmarks.  

2. Plot (a): Dynamic Response Magnification Factor RD(η)  
 • Vertical axis runs from 0 to about 5.5 and is labeled “Dynamic response magnification factor RD(η).”  
 • Five curves correspond to different damping ratios ξ:  
   – ξ = 5% (lightest damping) has the highest and sharpest peak, reaching just over 5 at η≈1.  
   – ξ = 10% peaks at roughly 3.5.  
   – ξ = 25% peaks near 2.  
   – ξ = 50% shows only a mild elevation above unity, about 1.2 at resonance.  
   – ξ = 100% (critical damping) does not display any peak and monotonically decreases from 1 at η=0 toward zero as η increases.  
 • To the left of η=1 (sub-resonant region), all curves rise from RD(0)=1 up toward their respective peaks. To the right (super-resonant) they decay monotonically back toward zero, converging toward low magnification at high frequency ratios.  

3. Plot (b): Phase Angle φ(η)  
 • Vertical axis runs from 0° at the bottom to 180° at the top, labeled “φ(η).”  
 • Again five curves for the same damping ratios ξ = 5%, 10%, 25%, 50% and 100%.  
 • All curves start at φ(0)=0° (response in phase with excitation at very low frequencies).  
 • At η=1 the phase for all curves passes through φ=90° (the vertical dashed and horizontal dashed lines intersect).  
 • Beyond resonance (η>1) each curve monotonically approaches 180°, indicating that at high frequencies the response is nearly exactly out of phase with the applied force.  
 • The light-damping curves (ξ=5%, 10%) exhibit a more abrupt transition through 90°, whereas heavily damped cases (ξ=50%, 100%) show a more gradual, less steep S-shaped progression from 0° to 180°.  

4. Caption and Context  
 Beneath the two subplots is the combined caption:  
 “Figure 2.4: Dynamic response magnification factor and phase angle for a damped system excited by a harmonic force.”

Frequent use of condensations is made in dynamic analysis. These require a certain exper- tise, because the selection of the reference nodes is critical. The same holds for kinematic constraints too.
 While a force at a distance a generates a moment P·, the inertia of an eccentric mass is given by m·2. DYNA takes this effect into account automatically for standard kinematic constraints. This, however, results in off diagonal mass matrix components, which necessitate the use of a consistent, i.e. not diagonalised, mass matrix. These do not need not only more memory, but can lead also to oscillation of solution through violation of the discrete maximum principle at small time steps that perform disturbingly. But as these matrices are not always acceptable, the user therefore can switch to the use of a diagonalised mass matrix, which then requires special care in the description of the constraints. When modeling rigid floor disks one should place the reference node as close as possible to the gravity or the shear centre in order to get the most realistic results.
 Kinematic constraints increase the band width considerably. The memory capacity can thus be quickly exceeded in cases of large systems or strongly recursive kinematic constraints.

DYNA employs very compact formulations of the element stiffnesses. The spring and boundary elements are in the classical form given and do not distinguish from those ones in programs ASE or STAR2.
 The beam element is a real finite element with a displacement accretion with Hermitian function of second redundancy (therefore cubical polynomials). That is considered at:
 – variable stiffnesses and location of centre of gravity
 – variable locations of shear centre
 – shear deformations over correction terms
 – optional warping force torsion
 – elastic bedding for pile elements
 – all beam loads from database
 The element produces for static load cases results also for internal sections.
 The QUAD shell element is available in the basic version (Hughes and/or Bathe-Dvorkin) or with "‘assumed strains"’. The default version of the QUAD includes the sixth degree of freedom (drilling perpendicular to the element plane) with a variational principle of the rotational field.
 The BRIC element is available in the basic version or with "‘assumed strains"’.
 Special provisions are available for so called "‘incompressible elements"’ for the dynamic anal- ysis of fluids with QUAD or BRIC elements.
 Hint
 DYNA does not support orthotropic material stiffness or orthotropic thickness properties.

For all elements a primary load case can be read, which can be used for the determination of the geometric stiffness. The second order theory effects are exact in those cases where the axial force does not change due to geometric nonlinear effects. For cable elements large de- formations of this primary load case are also accounted for. For warping torsion there are also contributions from bending and warping moments which have to be accounted for iteratively.
 Thus this approach may be used either for a buckling eigenvalue or for performing a linearized dynamic or static analysis based on the tangential stiffness. So it exceeds classical P-delta effects. This approach is faster by magnitudes compared to a general geometric non linear analysis.
 The eigen frequency of member with tension will thereby increase, while those of members under compression will decrease until they reach the value of zero for the buckling load. How- ever for cable elements the complete separation of geometric stiffness is not always a good approach, as this might generate negative eigenvalues in a buckling analysis. On the other side a buckling factor is defined as the factor of the loading. So it is generally foreseen for cables to split the prestress in two parts. One part is included in the general stiffness (this is the value defined with the element itself) and the difference from the actual primary estate to that general value is then used to form the geometric stiffness for the buckling analysis. If that general value is not defined and option CTRL PLC does not select otherwise, the primary estate will be taken as general prestress.
 For beam elements there are some extra effects for static load cases available. For analysis according 2nd order theory a primary load case (in many cases only with a constant normal force) may be added to the results for a total design case(CTRL PLC W2 3) or omitted to save incremental results which might be used for a linear superposition (CTRL PLC W2 1 = default) Further it is possible to calculate the incremental loading for beam elements automatically (CTRL PLC W2 7).

DYNA uses linear Algorithms for performance reasons. Some important non linear effects are available however:
 – For vehicle-structure interaction a moving contact condition is available
 – Spring elements can perform all non linear effects including explicit force-displacement relations.
 There is no extra iteration for the residual forces, thus the change of the stiffness should not become to large.
 These effects are also avaiable for a modal analysis if the used eigen values allow suffi- cient relative displacements of the spring nodes.
 – Beam elements can account for all non linear effects form an interaction of a structure with a steady-state or transient wind field. This includes galloping and flutter.
 – Cable, Truss and QUAD elements may account for relative flow velocities as well
 – For BRIC elements all nonlinear material models are available for the explicit integration scheme

This table defines a series of “records” used by SOFiSTiK (beyond the basics of HEAD, END and PAGE, which are documented in the general SOFiSTiK: ’Basics’ manual).  Each record has a unique two- to four-character name and an associated list of “items” (parameters or fields) that can be set when that record is called.  In a RAG/vector-store context, you would index each record name as an entity and each item as an attribute of that entity.  Below is a structured description of every record in the table:

1. SYST  
   • Purpose: Global system settings for a model run.  
   • Items (7):  
     – TYPE: system type identifier  
     – NCS: structural coordinate system flag  
     – PROB: problem identifier  
     – PHYS: physics code selector  
     – CS: cross-section or coordinate specification  
     – PLC: placement or local coordinate flag  
     – STAT: status or state control  

2. CTRL  
   • Purpose: Generic control record, often linked to iterative or solver options.  
   • Items (3):  
     – OPT: option flag or keyword  
     – VAL: primary numeric or logical value  
     – VAL2: secondary numeric or logical value  

3. GRP  
   • Purpose: Definition of element or node groups for load, boundary, or result processing.  
   • Items (13):  
     – NO: group number  
     – VAL: group value or type code  
     – CS: coordinate system reference  
     – FACS / FACP / FACM: various facet or face-associated identifiers  
     – HING: hinge or rotational release flag  
     – RADA / RADB: radial output or reference directions  
     – MODD: modification descriptor or secondary mode  
     – WIND: wind‐loading group flag  
     – LMAX: maximum load step or frequency  
     – NCSP: special constraint or coupling parameter  

4. MAT  
   • Purpose: Material definition record (isotropic, orthotropic, etc.).  
   • Items (14):  
     – NO: material number  
     – E: Young’s modulus  
     – MUE: Poisson’s ratio μ  
     – G: shear modulus  
     – K: bulk modulus  
     – GAM / GAMA: damping or gamma parameter  
     – ALFA: thermal expansion coefficient  
     – EY: secondary modulus (in orthotropic cases)  
     – MXY: Poisson’s ratio in plane XY  
     – OAL / OAF: optional alpha factors  
     – SPM: specific mass  
     – TITL: material title or description  

5. BMAT  
   • Purpose: “B‐mat” record for bi-material interfaces or special cohesive behavior.  
   • Items (12):  
     – NO: interface/material number  
     – C: cohesion or initial stiffness  
     – CT: contact type flag  
     – CRAC: crack initiation criterion  
     – YIEL: yield or plastic threshold  
     – MUE: Poisson’s ratio for interface  
     – COH: cohesive energy  
     – DIL: dilation angle or factor  
     – GAMB: gamma bending stiffness  
     – REF / MREF: reference values for normalization  
     – H: interface thickness  

6. SMAT  
   • Purpose: “S‐mat” record for soil or sediment materials (special constitutive model).  
   • Items (9):  
     – NO: material number  
     – LC: loading condition code  
     – EX: Young’s modulus for soils  
     – EY / EZ: secondary moduli in y and z  
     – RHOZ / RHOY: densities in principal directions  
     – ALF: alpha parameter (hardening)  
     – BET: beta parameter (dilation)  

7. MASS  
   • Purpose: Lumped or distributed mass properties on elements or nodes.  
   • Items (11):  
     – NO: identifier (element or mass case number)  
     – MX, MY, MZ: mass per unit length/area in X, Y, Z  
     – MXX, MYY, MZZ: rotational inertia components  
     – MXY, MXZ, MYZ: products of inertia  
     – MB: bulk mass or additional mass offset  

8. EIGE  
   • Purpose: Eigenvalue extraction settings (modal analysis).  
   • Items (8):  
     – NEIG: number of eigenvalues to extract  
     – TYPE: extraction method (e.g., standard, subspace)  
     – NITE: maximum iterations  
     – MITE: minimum iterations  
     – LMIN: lower bound of spectrum  
     – STOR: storage scheme selector  
     – LC / LCUP: Lanczos cycle length or update frequency  

9. MODD  
   • Purpose: Modal damping or mode-specific modifications.  
   • Items (5):  
     – NO: mode number or identifier  
     – D: damping factor  
     – A / B: Rayleigh damping coefficients  
     – PERS: personal or user-defined flag  

10. STEP  
    • Purpose: Load- or analysis-step control for nonlinearity, time integration, spectrum.  
    • Items (13):  
      – N: step number  
      – DT: time increment or load‐factor increment  
      – INT: integration scheme code  
      – A / B: step-specific parameters (e.g., B‐matrix factors)

This table defines the keyword-driven parameters for selecting and configuring the finite‐element analysis system (“SYST”) in the database.  It consists of four columns—Item, Description, Unit, and Default—and seven primary items.  Below is a breakdown of each:

1.  TYPE  (Unit: LIT, Default: REST)  
    •  Purpose: Chooses which FE system to use.  
    •  Options:  
       – REST – “use existing main system.”  
       – SECT – “use subsystem of a specific section,” in which case you must also supply SNO (section number).  
    •  Context: The system must already exist in the database (see “SYST”).  To restrict analysis to a predefined section mesh, issue  
       SYST SECT nnn  
       where nnn is the section’s ID; the corresponding FE-system is loaded from a separate subdirectory.  

2.  SNO  (Unit: —, Default: –)  
    •  Purpose: When TYPE=SECT, this integer identifies which section’s mesh and system to pull.  

3.  PROB  (Unit: LIT, Default: *)  
    •  Purpose: Defines the geometric theory used in the analysis.  
    •  Options:  
       – LINE – linear geometric theory (small strains and no geometric stiffness).  
       – TH2 – 2nd-order theory (small deflections, but includes stress-induced geometric stiffness).  
       – TH3 – 3rd-order theory (large deflections, small strains).  
    •  Context: If no primary load case (PLC) is defined, the analysis always falls back to LINE.  When a PLC is present, TH2 becomes the default.  TH3 is available only with explicit integration algorithms.  

4.  PHYS  (Unit: LIT, Default: LINE)  
    •  Purpose: Chooses the physical constitutive behavior—linear or various levels of nonlinear response.  
    •  Options:  
       – LINE – purely linear elasticity.  
       – NONL – fully nonlinear (all elements and materials follow nonlinear laws; explicit only).  
       – NSPR – nonlinear springs only.  
       – NMAT – nonlinear materials only.  
    •  Context: When nonlinear is selected, the code will read the appropriate stress–strain laws and safety factors from the INI-file of the chosen design code.  Only explicit integrators support full material nonlinearity.  

5.  CS  (Unit: —, Default: –)  
    •  Purpose: Indicates the construction stage whose properties are to be used.  
    •  Context: Material stiffness and initial stresses can change by construction stage; the analysis engine picks up stage-specific parameters.  

6.  PLC  (Unit: —, Default: –)  
    •  Purpose: Specifies the primary load case from which initial stresses (for geometric stiffness) and deformations are imported.  
    •  Context: Required if you want to enable TH2 or TH3 geometric theories—otherwise PROB reverts to LINE.  Also ties into the CTRL PLC mechanism for selecting load definitions.  

7.  STAT  (Unit: LIT, Default: –)  
    •  Purpose: Defines the overall “state” or design check to perform, which in turn presets factor combinations, safety margins, and applicable code rules.  
    •  Options:  
       – SERV – Serviceability check (deflection, crack width, etc.).  
       – ULTI – Ultimate limit state (strength, capacity).  
       – CALC – General nonlinear analysis (for custom scenarios or post-processing).  

Additional references:  
•  CTRL – governs how load cases (including PLC) are activated and combined.  
•  STEP – controls incremental solution steps and convergence criteria.  
•  GRP – defines element groups, material assignments, and output sets.  

Putting it all together, a complete command line might look like:  
“SYST REST PROB TH2 PHYS NONL CS 3 PLC 5 STAT ULTI”  
which would run a second-order, full-nonlinear, ultimate-limit analysis on the main system using construction stage 3 and primary load case 5.

This table defines the generic structure of a control-type input record used throughout the software (for CTRL itself as well as for related commands such as ECHO, GRP, MASS, EIGE, MODD, STEP, LC, CONT, HIST and EXTR).  It lays out seven fields (Item, Description, Unit, Default) and shows how they are to be interpreted whenever a user specifies control parameters via an OPT/VAL/V2–V6 scheme.

1. Item  
   • OPT   – Parameter mnemonic (literal text) that selects which internal calculation option is being modified or activated.  
   • VAL   – Primary argument for that option (numeric index, string or flag value).  
   • V2…V6 – Up to five additional arguments whose meaning depends on the specific OPT code.  

2. Description  
   • OPT – “Calculation parameter”: this is the keyword that tells the system which control action to perform (for example PLC, RLC, BTYP, WARP, QUAD, MCON, etc.).  
   • VAL – “Value of the parameter”: the main data required by the chosen OPT.  For a load case option (PLC), VAL would be the case number.  For a beam formulation (BTYP), VAL might be a bit-pattern integer.  
   • V2…V6 – “Secondary value(s) of the parameter”: used to pass flags, bit masks or supplementary numeric settings.  Their precise interpretation is defined in the contextual documentation for each OPT.  For example, with OPT=PLC, V2 toggles geometry vs. transient-analysis usage, V3 controls which beam stiffness terms enter the primary-load-case stiffness, V4 addresses cable buckling options, and so on.  

3. Unit  
   • OPT – Unit “LIT”, indicating a literal string or token.  
   • VAL,V2…V6 – Unit “—” (unitless or context-sensitive).  Numeric or integer values are assumed to be dimensionless flags or identifiers.  

4. Default  
   • “!” indicates that the field must be supplied by the user when the record is used.  It has no built-in fallback.  
   • “–” means optional: if the field is omitted, a default of zero or “off” is assumed by the code.  

Usage Notes  
• This template repeats across many modules: when you see any command that begins with an OPT field followed by VAL and optional V2…V6, you should refer back to the appropriate section of the manual for that specific OPT keyword.  
• See also the sections on ECHO (echo control), GRP (buckling length limit), MASS (mass matrix formulation), EIGE (eigenvalue extraction), MODD (mode damping), STEP (time stepping), LC (loadcases), CONT (continuation), HIST (history output) and EXTR (extreme value evaluation) for examples of how this general structure is reused.  
• By centralizing all control parameters into this uniform OPT/VAL/V2–V6 format, the software achieves a consistent user interface and allows future expansion (additional V-fields) with minimal changes to the parsing logic.

The input table defines the SOFiSTiK equation‐solver selection parameter (CTRL SOLV) in a compact four‐column format. It is intended for rapid look-up when setting up a finite‐element run. Below is a breakdown of its structure and contents:

1. Column Headers  
   • SOLV  
     – This identifies the controller keyword. All entries in the block fall under SOLV.  
   • Description  
     – A short text explaining what each code stands for—i.e. the name and nature of the solver.  
   • Unit  
     – The physical unit or type of the parameter. In this case it is “–” since the solver selection is dimensionless.  
   • Default  
     – The default integer code SOFiSTiK uses if no user override is supplied.

2. Parameter Block  
   Under the SOLV column there is a single sub‐entry called VAL. This indicates that SOLV takes a value (VAL) which selects among several predefined solver algorithms.

3. Default Setting  
   – Default VAL = 3  
     By default SOFiSTiK chooses code “3,” corresponding to the Direct Sparse LDL Solver.

4. Solver Codes and Descriptions  
   – 1  
     Description: Direct Skyline Solver (Gauss/Cholesky)  
     • Classical FE solver using skyline storage.  
     • Works best if the equation numbering is optimized for skyline (via CTRL OPTI 1 or 2).  
     • Can consume large amounts of memory for 3D models due to fill‐in in the skyline profile.  
     • No extra runtime parameters beyond correct node numbering.  

   – 2  
     Description: Iterative Sparse Solver (Conjugate Gradients)  
     • Employs preconditioned conjugate‐gradient iterations.  
     • Lowest storage requirement among all solvers.  
     • Often faster for large‐volume problems.  
     • Supports three preconditioning variants (diagonal scaling, incomplete Cholesky, incomplete inverse) selectable via V4 and V5/V6 thresholds.  
     • Parallel execution possible under HISOLV license (CTRL CORE).  

   – 3  
     Description: Direct Sparse LDL Solver  
     • State‐of‐the‐art direct solver based on sparse LDLᵀ factorization (e.g. Davis’s algorithm).  
     • Mesh generators default to an equation numbering that minimizes fill‐in.  
     • No additional parameters needed.  

   – 4  
     Description: Direct Parallel Sparse Solver (PARDISO)  
     • Intel MKL-based high‐performance, multi‐threaded solver.  
     • Typically provides the shortest compute times.  
     • Does not require prior equation reordering (CTRL OPTI can be set to 0).  
     • Cannot export the factorized matrix for reuse (incompatible with ELLA).  

5. Usage Notes (for RAG Vector Store Context)  
   – This table is the canonical reference for automated solver selection in preprocessing scripts.  
   – The “Default” column flags the solver the engine will pick when (CTRL SOLV) is omitted.  
   – Clients building RAG embeddings should tokenize solver names, numeric codes, and default values as discrete metadata fields for rapid retrieval.  
   – Downstream agents can use the “Unit” column to recognize that this parameter is dimensionless, avoiding misinterpretation as a physical quantity.

The table under “CTRL SOLV 2” defines all of the input parameters you must supply when you choose the iterative (conjugate‐gradient) solver in SOFiSTiK.  In essence it tells you which keywords to set, what each one means, the allowable ranges or enumerations, the units (all dimensionless here), and what default value is applied if you don’t override it.

1. SOLV VAL (solver type)  
   – Keyword: SOLV VAL  
   – Value “2” selects the iterative equation solver.  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: “!” (mandatory to specify in a run; the program will not assume the iterative solver by default)

2. V2 Maximum number of iterations  
   – Keyword: SOLV V2  
   – Specifies the upper limit on CG steps.  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: “*” (no preset default — you must supply a value suitable for your problem size)

3. V3 Tolerance in numeric digits  
   – Keyword: SOLV V3  
   – Convergence criterion expressed as the number of correct digits in the residual (allowed range from 5 to 15).  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: “*” (user must set; note that adjusting this too loosely risks inaccurate solutions, while tightening it may increase iteration count)

4. V4 Type of preconditioning  
   – Keyword: SOLV V4  
   – Enumeration of three supported schemes:  
     • 0 = Diagonal Scaling  
       – Simplest and fastest to build but typically requires many more CG iterations  
     • 1 = Incomplete Cholesky (default)  
       – Builds a partial Cholesky factor, omitting “fill-in.” Offers a good balance of memory and speed  
     • 2 = Incomplete Inverse  
       – Constructs an approximate inverse; generally slower convergence than 1, but can outperform on very dense matrices  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: 1

5. V5 Threshold value of preconditioning  
   – Keyword: SOLV V5  
   – Relative cut-off used during the formation of the preconditioner to drop small terms (between 0 and 1).  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: “*” (user must test different thresholds to find the best trade-off for their stiffness matrix sparsity)

6. V6 Maximum bandwidth in preconditioning  
   – Keyword: SOLV V6  
   – Forces the incomplete factor to consider only a specified half-bandwidth around the main diagonal.  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: “*” (again, test various settings to limit memory use without overly harming convergence)

Notes and Recommendations (from the SOFiSTiK context):  
– The iterative solver is most attractive when memory is tight or for very large 3D volume meshes.  
– Always be cautious about loosening the tolerance (V3) — the code’s hints stress that you should validate results against a direct solver.  
– Try Incomplete Cholesky (V4=1) first; only move to other pre-conditioning strategies if you encounter convergence or performance issues.  
– Tune V5 and V6 systematically (“parameter sweep”) to match the sparsity pattern of your specific finite‐element matrix.

1. SOLV

Row breakdown  
----------  
• WERT = 4

  – “4” maps to PARDISO, SOFiSTiK’s direct parallel sparse solver.  

• Description = “Direct parallel sparse solver”

  – It does not require a prior equation renumbering (CTRL OPTI can even be set to 0 to save memory during system generation).

--------------------------------------

 • Direct Skyline Solver (Gauss/Cholesky)

 Iterative Solver (Conjugate Gradients)
 One advantage of the iterative solver lies in its reduced requirements for storage, but it may also provide reduced computing time compared to the previous two types especially in case of large volume structures.
 • Direct Sparse Solver
 These types of solvers correspond to state of technology. A quite efficient version based on the work of Davis [7] is available as well as a direct parallel solver PARDISO.
 The advantage of the direct solvers is especially given in case of multiple right hand sides, as the effort for solving them is very small compared to the triangulization of the equation system. Thus they are the first choice for any dynamic analysis or in case of many load cases.
 In order to minimize computational effort, the solvers need an optimized sequence of equation numbers. This optimization step is usually performed during system generation. The programs SOFIMSHA/C by default always create a sequence which is suitable for the direct sparse solver (3). The solvers (1) or (2) however require a skyline oriented numbering which may be obtained using the option (CTRL OPTI 1) or (CTRL OPTI 2) during system generation. The correct setting will be checked and a warning will be issued in case a correct numbering is not available.
 The iterative (CTRL SOLV 2) and the parallel sparse solver (CTRL SOLV 4) can be run in par- allel providing an additional reduction in computing time. The table shown defines the single sub-parameter of the “CTRL CORE” command in SOFiSTiK, which controls how many threads the program will use when parallel processing is active. Below is a breakdown of each column in the table and a detailed explanation of the parameter’s semantics, defaults and interactions with other settings.

1. Table Columns  
   • CORE  
     – This column shows the name of the sub-parameter under the main “CTRL CORE” control record.  
     – In our case there is only one entry, named “VAL.”  
   • Description  
     – A brief, human-readable description of what the parameter does.  
     – “Number of used threads” indicates exactly that: how many CPU threads SOFiSTiK should spawn.  
   • Unit  
     – The unit column is “—” because the parameter is a simple integer count of threads, not a physical quantity.  
   • Default  
     – An asterisk “*” here means “automatic.” When you do not explicitly set a thread count, SOFiSTiK chooses a default based on the hardware and environment settings (see below).

2. Purpose of CTRL CORE VAL  
   When you request a parallel run (either via a solver inherently running in parallel or via parallel element processing), the system needs to know how many threads to allocate. CTRL CORE VAL is the mechanism by which you can:  
   – Override the default number of threads for the current analysis.  
   – Temporarily limit or expand parallelism on a per-run basis.  
   – Suppress parallel execution altogether by setting VAL to 1 (or 0 in certain contexts).

3. How the Default “*” Value Is Determined  
   If you leave VAL set to “*,” SOFiSTiK will pick a thread count in this order (highest to lowest priority):  
   a) System Query  
      • The software queries the operating system to find the number of physical processor cores.  
      • That core count becomes the initial default thread count.  
   b) Environment or Global Definition  
      • If you have set the environment variable SOF_NUM_THREADS or the equivalent parameter in sofistik.def, that number replaces the OS-detected default.  
   c) Explicit CTRL CORE Statement  
      • If, in the same run input, you include a CTRL CORE VAL or CTRL CORE VAL[%] command, that value temporarily overrides b) and a).  
   Note: Steps b) and c) do not in themselves request parallel processing—they merely adjust the thread count should a parallel task be invoked. Actual activation still depends on:  
   • The chosen analysis type must support parallel execution.  
   • A valid HISOLV (ISOL granule) license must be available.  

4. Suppressing Parallel Execution  
   Even if your hardware and license support parallel runs, you can force single-threaded operation by setting CTRL CORE VAL to 1 (or 0 on some platforms). This is useful for debugging or when running on systems where multithreading causes overhead.  

5. Practical Notes  
   • Always verify that your solver or task supports CTRL SOLV or independent element-level parallelism.  
   • If you see performance not scaling with threads, check licensing (HISOLV), OS support (thread affinity), and whether the analysis is parallel-enabled.  
   • Use environment variables or global config for site-wide defaults; reserve CTRL CORE statements for exceptions or benchmarking.

The table provided summarizes four of SOFiSTiK’s linear equation solvers, their control codes (CTRL SOLV), and the licensing requirements for both serial and parallel execution. This information is essential when configuring a Run‐Analysis‐Go (RAG) workflow that may leverage multi‐core or multi‐processor hardware under the correct license provisions.

1. Columns and Entries  
   • Solver: Lists the name and type of solver.  
     – “Skyline Gauss/Cholesky”: A direct solver utilizing skyline storage.  
     – “Iterativ”: An iterative algorithm, typically Krylov‐type methods.  
     – “Sparse LDL (default)”: The default sparse solver employing an LDLᵀ factorization.  
     – “Sparse Parallel (Pardiso)”: A parallelized sparse solver based on Pardiso technology.  
   • CTRL SOLV: Numeric code used in SOFiSTiK input to select the solver.  
     – Skyline Gauss/Cholesky → 1  
     – Iterativ → 2  
     – Sparse LDL (default) → 3  
     – Sparse Parallel (Pardiso) → 4  
   • License (Serial): Indicates which license or granule is needed to run the solver in single‐threaded mode.  
     – Skyline Gauss/Cholesky: no special license (denoted “—”).  
     – Iterativ: requires HISOLV.  
     – Sparse LDL: no special license (default solver).  
     – Sparse Parallel: requires HISOLV even for serial runs.  
   • License (Parallel): Indicates the license needed to enable multi‐threaded or distributed computation.  
     – Skyline Gauss/Cholesky: not applicable (n.a.), parallel not supported.  
     – Iterativ: HISOLV required.  
     – Sparse LDL: n.a. (parallel version not offered).  
     – Sparse Parallel: HISOLV required to unlock parallel capabilities.

2. Context for Parallel Computing  
   SOFiSTiK can automatically switch to a parallel execution path wherever supported—provided the underlying hardware and operating system facilitate multi‐core processing, and an adequate SOFiSTiK license (specifically the ISOL granule, HISOLV) is available. Merely specifying a parallel‐capable solver (e.g. CTRL SOLV=4) does not guarantee multi‐threading: the actual decision depends on the combination of solver support, license entitlement, and explicit thread settings.

3. Thread Count Determination  
   When parallel computing is active, the number of threads is chosen in ascending order of priority:  
   a) System query of physical processor cores defines the default thread count.  
   b) The SOF_NUM_THREADS environment variable (or sofistik.def parameter) can override the default.  
   c) A temporary per‐run override via “CTRL CORE NN” or “CTRL CORE NN[%]” sets the thread count explicitly.  
   • Setting threads to 1 (or 0) forcibly disables parallel execution, even for solvers that support it.

4. Practical Implications for RAG  
   – For purely serial workflows on any machine, no HISOLV license is strictly needed if the default Sparse LDL (CTRL SOLV=3) or Skyline Gauss/Cholesky (CTRL SOLV=1) solvers suffice.  
   – To exploit multi‐core performance (especially for large sparse problems), one should select “Sparse Parallel (Pardiso)” via CTRL SOLV=4 and ensure a valid HISOLV license.  
   – Fine-tuning thread usage through environment variables or CTRL CORE statements allows balancing memory overheads against compute throughput.  
   – Embedding this table into a RAG vector store will streamline solver selection logic, license checks, and automatic thread management directives during automated pre‐ and post‐processing steps.

The SMAT record is used within the Scaled Boundary Finite Element Method (SBFEM) to prescribe how material properties vary for soil‐structure interaction models.  In three‐dimensional analyses the soil’s material number is inherited from the SBFEM‐QUAD element, while in two‐dimensional plane‐strain or axisymmetric setups it comes from the SBFEM‐BOUN element.  If no boundary element material number is explicitly assigned in 2D, the default soil material number “1” is used.  The following table lists all SMAT parameters (items), their physical meaning, associated units, and default values.

Column Definitions  
• Item: an abbreviated parameter name used in the SMAT input record.  
• Description: a concise statement of what property each parameter controls.  
• Unit: the measurement unit for each parameter, where “—” indicates a dimensionless coefficient.  
• Default: the value assumed when the user does not explicitly specify the parameter.

Row‐by‐Row Parameter Details  
1. NO (Material number)  
   – Description: Identifies which material definition from the global database is linked to the soil domain.  
   – Unit: dimensionless.  
   – Default: 1 (the first material entry).  

2. LC (Characteristic Length)  
   – Description: Controls the length scale used to normalize inhomogeneity functions in the SBFEM formulation.  
   – Unit: meters (m).  
   – Default: no fixed value (“!” indicates this must be provided by the user).  

3. EX (Elasticity coefficient in X‐direction)  
4. EY (Elasticity coefficient in Y‐direction)  
5. EZ (Elasticity coefficient in Z‐direction)  
   – Description: Define how elastic stiffness varies along each principal axis. These coefficients factor into the power‐law or exponential inhomogeneity profiles when evaluating spatially varying Young’s modulus.  
   – Unit: dimensionless.  
   – Default: 0 (uniform elasticity, no variation).  

6. RHOX, RHOY, RHOZ (Density coefficients in X, Y, Z directions)  
   – Description: Analogous to EX/EY/EZ but applied to the mass density field; control directional inhomogeneity of soil density.  
   – Unit: dimensionless.  
   – Default: 0 (constant density).  

7. ALF (Inhomogeneity of elasticity)  
   – Description: A global scalar that further modulates the overall variation of elastic properties, often combined with EX/EY/EZ terms to yield complex spatial profiles.  
   – Unit: dimensionless.  
   – Default: 0 (no additional inhomogeneity).  

8. BET (Inhomogeneity of density)  
   – Description: A global scalar applied to density variations, enabling custom density distributions throughout the soil.  
   – Unit: dimensionless.  
   – Default: 0 (homogeneous density).  

Usage Context  
When building an SBFEM‐based soil‐structure interaction model, the user first assigns a soil material number via NO (or inherits it automatically).  The characteristic length LC must then be set to establish the spatial scale of inhomogeneity.  If the soil is assumed homogeneous, all EX/EY/EZ and RHOX/RHOY/RHOZ entries remain at their zero defaults, and ALF/BET remain zero.  Nonzero entries in these fields produce anisotropic or spatially varying elastic and density profiles, which the solver accounts for during stiffness and mass matrix assembly. This SMAT table thus provides a concise, flexible framework for defining complex material distributions in SBFEM analyses.

The table below defines the keyword‐value pairs used to set up an eigenvalue or buckling analysis (EIGE).  Each row describes one input parameter (“Item”), its purpose (“Description”), the units in which its value must be supplied (“Unit”), and the default if the user does not override it (“Default”).  In combination these entries control how many eigenvalues are found, which algorithm is used, how many iterations are performed, how results are stored, and any special options (missing mass, buckling, restart, etc.).

Item     • Description                                                                         • Unit         • Default

1. NEIG  
   – Number of sought eigenvalues.  
   – Specifies how many lowest (or shifted) eigenvalues to compute.  
   – Unit: — (integer)  
   – Default: Required argument (!).  

2. TYPE  
   – Method for the eigenvalue computation.  A literal string (LIT) selects one of:  
       • REST – eigenvalues already available (imported from a prior run or external program)  
       • SIMU – simultaneous vector iteration (default)  
       • LANC – Lanczos method  
       • BUCK – buckling vector iteration  
       • BULL – buckling Lanczos  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: SIMU  

3. NITE  
   – Number of iterations (or, in the Lanczos method, the number of Lanczos vectors).  
   – Controls subspace dimension in the simultaneous vector iteration.  By default NITE = min(NEIG + 2, total unknowns).  
   – Unit: — (integer)  
   – Default: Automatically chosen (*)  

4. MITE  
   – Maximum number of iterations and associated options for the chosen algorithm.  
   – In vector iteration, the iteration stops when either this limit is reached or the highest eigenvalue changes by less than 1e-5 from one cycle to the next.  Default max (15, 2 × NITE).  
   – Unit: — (integer)  
   – Default: Automatically chosen (*)  

5. LMIN  
   – Eigenvalue shift (rad²/sec²).  
   – Adds a constant diagonal perturbation to the stiffness matrix to shift all eigenvalues by LMIN.  Useful for structures with zero‐frequency rigid‐body modes or for Sturm‐sequence counting.  
   – Unit: rad²/sec²  
   – Default: 0  

6. STOR  
   – Number of eigenforms (mode shapes) to be stored in the database.  
   – These can later be retrieved as load cases for graphical deformation plots or modal force evaluation (requires associated stresses/forces).  
   – Unit: — (integer)  
   – Default: NEIG  

7. LC  
   – Load‐case number assigned to the lowest eigenform.  
   – Subsequent modes are stored in ascending load‐case order.  
   – Unit: — (integer)  
   – Default: 1  

8. OPT  
   – Miscellaneous options:  
       – 1: Include “missing mass” rigid‐body modes as extra load cases (up to three), automatically activated when uniform ground acceleration is applied.  
   – Other flags may enable special restart or automatic base‐case generation (LC BASE AUTO).  
   – Unit: — (bit mask/integer)  
   – Default: Automatically chosen (*)  

Notes / Cross-references:  
• Use TYPE REST when importing eigenvalues from programs such as ASE.  
• For buckling analysis, either specify TYPE BUCK (vector‐iteration) or BULL (Lanczos).  
• Selecting CTRL PLC causes geometric initial stiffness to be included, introducing zero frequencies as you approach a buckling state.  
• For modal response evaluation, all mode shapes must be stored with element stresses or forces.  
• The Lanczos method is preferred for large NEIG, achieving good accuracy when NITE≥2 × NEIG; setting NITE=NEIG usually degrades higher modes.  
• Shifted‐mode (“sturm”) counting reports number of skipped eigenvalues via sign changes of det(K–λM).

The table, titled “Overview of the algorithms,” provides a side-by-side comparison of two prominent methods for solving structural eigenvalue problems—simultaneous vector iteration and the Lanczos algorithm—across seven key criteria. This summary is particularly useful for deciding which method to invoke in a RAG-enabled finite-element workflow when requesting EIGE (eigenvalue) analysis.

1. Number of Eigenvalues  
   - Vector iteration excels at calculating a moderate number of eigenvalues. It is robust when you only need a handful of modes (e.g., for low-order vibration or buckling studies).  
   - Lanczos is designed to handle a high count of eigenvalues efficiently, making it the preferred choice when you must extract many modes from large models.

2. Range of Eigenvalues  
   - In vector iteration, extracting widely separated eigenvalues may trigger convergence issues via the Ritz-Step process (“Ritz-Step problematic”). Care must be taken if your spectrum spans both low and high frequencies.  
   - Lanczos shows no such sensitivity; it can capture a broad span of the spectrum without stability concerns.

3. Multiple Eigenvalues  
   - Both methods correctly resolve repeated (multiple) eigenvalues without special modifications, so degenerate modes or symmetrical structures do not pose a problem in either approach.

4. Missing Eigenvalues  
   - Vector iteration very rarely fails to converge on any requested eigenvalue. This makes it more reliable for critical safety checks when missing a mode is unacceptable.  
   - Lanczos can occasionally skip certain eigenvalues (labeled “rare”), so it is advisable to verify completeness if the full modal set is needed.

5. Negative Eigenvalues  
   - Vector iteration can accommodate negative eigenvalues, which are common in geometric stiffness (buckling) analyses.  
   - Lanczos does not support negative eigenvalues, limiting its use strictly to positive-definite mass-stiffness vibration problems.

6. Memory Requirement  
   - The memory footprint of vector iteration is moderate: it needs storage for a small subspace of trial vectors (default subspace size is NEIG+2 or the total number of DOFs, whichever is smaller).  
   - Lanczos requires a high amount of memory because it builds and stores a large Lanczos basis when extracting many modes.

7. Speed  
   - Vector iteration is of moderate speed; convergence may take multiple iterations (up to max(15, 2·NITE)) especially if the shift or subspace size is not optimized.  
   - Lanczos is fast when many eigenvalues are sought and the Lanczos subspace (NITE) is at least twice the number of desired modes. Under these conditions, Lanczos significantly outperforms vector iteration in runtime.

In practice, if your problem demands only a few modes, includes negative eigenvalues (buckling), or runs on hardware with limited memory, vector iteration is the safer choice. For large-scale vibration analyses where hundreds of modes are required and the spectrum is strictly positive, Lanczos offers superior speed and robustness.

Below is a structured, detailed description of the five parameters defined in the MODD (modal damping) record. This description can be used to index or tag the table in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store. Where relevant, contextual notes drawn from the surrounding manual text have been included.  

1. Item “NO”  
   • Name: NO  
   • Role: Specifies which eigenvalue(s) the damping definition applies to.  
   • Description: “Number of the eigenvalue.” If omitted or set to “all,” the damping settings are applied to every mode. In modal analysis, each mode (eigenform) derives a separate modal damping value; selecting a specific NO targets a single eigenform.  
   • Unit: Not applicable (—)  
   • Default Value: “all”  

2. Item “D”  
   • Name: D  
   • Role: Direct Lehr’s modal damping factor.  
   • Description: “Direct Lehr’s modal damping.” When entered, this single value overwrites any group damping in GRP records or explicit damper elements. It corresponds to Lehr’s damping factor D directly, rather than being computed via A/B coefficients. In eigen‐ analysis, D corresponds to the modal damping ratio for the specified mode(s).  
   • Unit: Not applicable (—)  
   • Default Value: 0  

3. Item “A”  
   • Name: A  
   • Role: Mass‐proportional damping coefficient.  
   • Description: “Mass proportional damping.” In direct time integration (no eigenanalysis), modal damping does not exist by default and must be represented by a combination of mass‐ and stiffness‐ proportional damping. The A parameter multiplies the mass matrix to produce damping forces proportional to velocity.  
   • Unit: 1/sec  
   • Default Value: 0  

4. Item “B”  
   • Name: B  
   • Role: Stiffness‐proportional damping coefficient.  
   • Description: “Stiffness proportional damping.” Also used only in direct integration schemes. B multiplies the stiffness matrix; damping forces are proportional to displacements. Typical practice is to choose A and B so that the logarithmic decrement δ is approximately constant between two frequencies f₁ and f₂. The relation involves circular frequencies ω = 2π·f and the modal damping ratio ξ:  
     ξ = (A + B·ω²) / (2·ω)  
   • Unit: sec  
   • Default Value: 0  

5. Item “PERS”  
   • Name: PERS  
   • Role: Persistence flag for damping definitions.  
   • Description: “Persistent value.” A logical switch (Y/N or YE/NO) that determines whether the damping definition remains active across subsequent analyses or is reset. If set to Y, newly computed modal damping does not overwrite the stored entries in the database.  
   • Unit: Literal flag (LIT)  
   • Default Value: Y  

Contextual Notes:  
• In pure modal analysis, user‐entered D (Lehr’s damping) or A/B definitions are diagonalized along with the mass and stiffness matrices. Each resulting eigenform acquires a distinct modal damping ratio.  
• If only a logarithmic decrement δ is known (e.g. from literature values of 1–2% for plastic concrete or 0.4–1% for bolted steel), it can be converted to A/B using the target frequency. For instance, to achieve δ=10% at f=5 Hz, one could choose A=1.0 s⁻¹ or B=0.001 s.  
• Always specify damping values either as absolute numbers or with explicit “%” units. Failure to supply units may lead to ambiguous or incorrect damping assignments.  
• See also the records ECHO, CTRL, GRP and EIGE for complementary control options, group damping overrides and eigenvalue extraction controls.

         – nn: Any integer code pointing to an influence load case (e.g. for separate ground accelerations).  
      • Notes: In modal superposition with spectra (CTRL STYP), BASE controls how static components combine with dynamic modal responses.  
   5. MODB  
      • Description: “Modal base load case number.”  
      • Unit: —  
      • Default: –  
      • Notes: In a modal analysis where each eigenform may have its own distinct loading (e.g. wind‐induced modes), MODB specifies the load‐case index for the first eigenform; subsequent modes pull from consecutive case numbers.  
   6. TITL  
      • Description: “Identifier of the load case.”  
      • Unit: Lit32 (a 32-character literal string)  
      • Default: –  
      • Notes: A free‐text label that can help users track or document load cases in output listings.

3. Contextual Integration  
   – Transient Analysis (see STEP): All defined LCs plus their time functions run concurrently; CONT may define special contact conditions for moving loads.  
   – Static/Steady‐State Analysis (see ECHO, CTRL, HIST): Periodic loads are converted per Section 2.4; separate LCs can be combined via statistical superposition (CTRL STYP) or simple summation (BASE STAT).  
   – Spectral Loading: Where a response spectrum is attached, DYNA interpolates across all spectra, scales by user‐specified CRIT parameters, and merges via BASE and CTRL settings.  

See also the related keywords GRP (load grouping), MASS (mass assignments), EIGE/EIGE (eigenmode controls), EXTR (extraction options) for completing a fully detailed RAG-indexed description of DYNA’s load definition.

See also: ECHO, CTRL, GRP, MASS, EIGE, MODD, STEP, CONT, HIST, EXTR
 LC
 The loading in DYNA is subdivided in load cases identified by a number. Each load case can be assigned in program SOFiLOAD loadings, time-functions or a response spectrum. The use of the load cases differs according to the computational procedure:
 1. Transient analysis
 During a time variation analysis (STEP N > 0) all the selected load cases and their functions define the time dependence of the loading and the starting time. All functions act with their loads simultaneously upon the structure. DYNA allows the extra definition of a contact condition CONT for a moving load.
 2. Static or steady-state analysis
 In case of steady-state analysis the periodical loads are converted to corresponding re- sponses according to Section 2.4. In case of static analysis the load cases are analysed separately.
 If spectra are defined, DYNA computes by double interpolation of all the spectra a system response, which is then superimposed by statistical methods according to the input for CTRL STYP.
 With BASE STAT an static load cases is added to the modal superposition completely. With BASE AUTO the fraction of the load case according to the "‘missing mass method"’ is evalu- ated. The load case with the equivalent forces of the accelerations has to be calculated be- forehand. BASE with a number is used to introduce influence functions, needed for separated ground accelerations.
 For a modal analysis the general case is to apply the same load vector for all eigenforms. However if every eigenform should obtain a separate loading as in a modal wind analysis, the item MODB allows to specify the load case number for the loading to the first eigen form. All following eigenforms will be associated to the consecutive load case numbers.
 In this case there is a special feature for spectral loading:
 For the load cases the user defined parameter CRIT will be evaluated. If it is zero, no evaluation will be taken from the spectra. The response is 1.0. If defined otherwise the period of the eigenforms will be scaled with that value. Thus for a Wind spectrum this value is to be defined with Ltrb/men/ or z/men/ .

The table below defines the keyword‐based inputs for the CONT record in SOFiLOAD, which governs a single moving contact point (e.g. a wheel or axle) that travels along a structure (bridge, rail, roadway).  Each row corresponds to one parameter:

1. Item  
   – The keyword used in the CONT command.  

2. Description  
   – A concise explanation of what the parameter controls.  

3. Unit  
   – Physical unit, if applicable. A dash (“—”) indicates a dimensionless or integer value.  

4. Default  
   – The value assumed if the keyword is omitted. A dash indicates “no default.”  

Detailed parameter breakdown:

• TYPE  
  Description: “Selected contact value (obsoleted).”  
  Unit: LIT (literal string)  
  Default: none  
  Notes: Retained for backward compatibility; superseded by more flexible definitions using REF / NR / FUNC.  

• REF  
  Description: Identifier of a reference axis for load trains.  
  Unit: — (integer or user‐defined label)  
  Default: 0  
  Notes: Specifies which axis or alignment the moving contact will follow. When you set up multiple parallel lanes or tracks via the AXIS or GAX commands, REF selects one of them.  

• NR  
  Description: Number of an edge element.  
  Unit: —  
  Default: none  
  Notes: Selecting a boundary or edge element number automatically picks up all its constituent nodes in sequence. You may also concatenate multiple edge elements explicitly via FUNC records.  

• V  
  Description: Travel speed of the contact point.  
  Unit: m/sec  
  Default: none  
  Notes: If V and a reference axis are defined, SOFiLOAD computes the time value for each node by dividing the cumulative distance along the axis by V (plus the optional TMIN).  

• YEX  
  Description: Local eccentricity (lateral offset) of the contact point from the nominal node line.  
  Unit: m  
  Default: 0.0  
  Notes: A positive or negative offset in the local y-direction allows modeling wheel flange thickness or pavement edge effects.  

• TMIN  
  Description: Time at the start of travel.  
  Unit: sec  
  Default: 0.0  
  Notes: All automatically generated time­-node associations will be offset by this value.  

• LCUV  
  Description: Load case for vertical track irregularities.  
  Unit: —  
  Default: none  
  Notes: Attach a user‐defined load function that prescribes absolute vertical displacements at the contact point as a function of travel time.  

• LCUT  
  Description: Load case for transverse track irregularities.  
  Unit: —  
  Default: none  
  Notes: Similar to LCUV but for lateral displacements (side‐to‐side “uneven pavement”).  

• LCUR  
  Description: Load case for rotational track irregularities.  
  Unit: —  
  Default: none  
  Notes: Defines additional rotation (tilt) at the contact point as the load moves.  

Additional remarks:  
- Interpolation: At any instant, the contact‐point displacement is obtained by linear interpolation of the active nodal values on the selected edge. Nodal loads (external point loads) are only applied if the node number is set to 0.  
- Load trains: When used with a TRAI record in SOFiLOAD, multiple axles follow each other at fixed spacings—the CONT definition is then applied to every axle in the train.  
- Related commands: ECHO (output control), CTRL (dynamic‐analysis settings), GRP (node/element grouping), MASS (lumped masses), EIGE (eigenmodes), MODD (mode‐based damping), STEP (time‐step control), LC (assigning loads to cases), HIST (history output), EXTR (extraction definitions).  
- Example usage is provided in “dyna9_travelling_loads.dat” and “loadtrains.dat” under the SOFiLOAD distribution.

 CONT
 Dynamic contact is governed by a changing location of contact point within time, as it is given in the case of a vehicle travelling along a bridge.
 This record allows the definition of the development in time of the contact point and a mecha- nism to create loads based on current deformations of the system.
 For the time dependant location you have to select a sequence of nodes and specify the time value for each node when the contact point is exactly at that point. In most cases the selection of the number NO of a boundary/edge element will select all nodes in the given sequence. However explicit definitions with FUNC (program SOFiLOAD) records and mixing and concate- nation of several elements is possible. Defining a travelling speed V will generate all the needed time values from the distance either directly or taken along the reference axis and the optional start time TMIN.
 If the load case has a load train created within SOFiLOAD, all loads of the train will follow each other with the appropriate distance. If the load train has also structural- or visualisation objects created via the TREX command, the nodes of those objects will receive the current coordinates as displacements and the absolute velocities. Only the point loads are processed by the CONT command.
 The three load cases LCUV, LCUT and LCUR allow to introduce track irregularities or uneven pavements as additional displacements or rotations for the contact-point. The load functions of these load cases must have the absolute displacements as a function of the travelling time of the load reference point.
 The reference displacement at the contact point is obtained by a linear interpolation between the adjacent nodes. The loading at the contact point is similarly distributed between the ad- jacent nodes. External nodal loads are placed at the contact point only if the node number is specified as 0.

The input table is the field‐by‐field definition of the HIST input record. HIST is used to request time histories of up to 32 quantities (spring forces, moments, stresses, etc.), store them in the database for post-processing (with DYNR), print them directly, or dump them to an external file.  Regardless of output mode, HIST always computes and reports the global maximum and minimum of each requested curve.  

The table is organized into four columns:  
• Item – the keyword or identifier that must appear in the HIST record  
• Description – a brief semantic explanation of what the field controls  
• Unit – the physical or literal type of the field’s argument  
• Default – the value assumed if the field is omitted  

1. TYPE  
   – Description: Specifies which result quantity to record. A code or literal (see the main “result value” table for available options: e.g. P, PT, M, PX, etc.).  
   – Unit: LIT (a literal code)  
   – Default: “S”  

2. FROM  
   – Description: The smallest node or element number in the range over which this result is collected.  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: 1  

3. TO  
   – Description: The largest node or element number in the range.  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: same as FROM (i.e. a single index if TO is omitted)  

4. INC  
   – Description: Either an index increment (for element numbering) or, when TYPE refers to stresses, the stress‐point identifier (SPT) within each section. INC=0 is allowed only when FROM=TO; INC>0 denotes a change relative to prestressing force or a particular SPT.  
   – Unit: –/Lit  
   – Default: 1  

5. RESU  
   – Description: Controls how HIST outputs the data. Must be one of three suboptions:  
     • SAVE – save values in the internal DYNR database (no immediate print)  
     • PRIN – save and also print the values to the output file  
     • PHAS – for frequency‐response requests: save both amplitudes and phases  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: SAVE  

6. LCST  
   – Description: Case number under which to store the time history in the database.  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: “*” (i.e. use the current load case)  

7. XREF  
   – Description: For beam‐type elements, the reference station or section (measured from the element start). If negative, the value is taken as a fraction of the total beam length (e.g. –1.0 for the downstream end).  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: 0.0  

8. YREF  
   – Description: Secondary reference coordinate (for summing spring force components or defining in‐plane distances when computing moments/dP/P).  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: 0.0  

9. ZREF  
   – Description: Tertiary reference coordinate or, when TYPE involves DP/P ratios, the width over which ΔP is computed.  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: 0.0  

10. DUMP  
   – Description: Name of the external file (up to 48 characters) in which to write the time history dump, instead of or in addition to database storage.  
   – Unit: Lit48  
   – Default: “–” (no dump file)  

Notes drawn from surrounding context:  
• Spring‐force entries (P, PT, M, PX/PY/PZ, PT/P, DP/P) make it easy to track absolute and ratio quantities for vehicle–structure interaction.  
• Stress requests require INC to identify the SPT within a section.  
• HIST always prints computed maxima/minima, even if output is only being saved, ensuring rapid sanity checks on dynamic runs.  

See also: ECHO, CTRL, GRP, MASS, EIGE, MODD, STEP, LC, CONT, EXTR.

The table under discussion (Table 3.19: “Possible literals for TYPE”) enumerates all of the valid “TYPE” specifiers that can be used when defining what quantities are to be collected by the HIST record in a reading or post-processing run.  In a RAG (Retriever–Augmented Generator) or vector-store context, you would index each TYPE literal as an independent token or key, with its associated meaning, so that downstream retrieval can map user queries (e.g. “spring forces,” “rotations,” “angular acceleration”) directly to the correct TYPE code(s).

Summary of columns and contents  
• TYPE literal: one or more alphanumeric characters (sometimes including “/” or “P”) that code a particular field.  
• Meaning: human-readable description of the physical quantity referenced by that literal.

Groupings of TYPE codes:

1.  Displacements and rotations  
   – UX, UY, UZ  
     • Displacements in global X, Y, Z directions.  
   – RX, RY, RZ  
     • Rotations about the global X, Y, Z axes.

2.  Velocities and angular velocity  
   – VX, VY, VZ  
     • Translational velocities along X, Y, Z.  
   – (no literal prefix shown for angular velocity; in practice, “WX, WY, WZ” or simply “W” is often implied)  
     • Angular (spin) velocity.

3.  Accelerations and angular acceleration  
   – AX, AY, AZ  
     • Translational accelerations.  
   – (again, an implied angular-acceleration code, e.g. “AWX, AWY, AWZ,” or “AA,” denotes rotational acceleration.)

4.  Spring forces and moments  
   – P, PT, M  
     • P: main spring force.  
     • PT: transverse (lateral) spring force.  
     • M: spring moment.

5.  Spring force global components  
   – PX, PY, PZ  
     • The global X, Y, Z components of the total spring force vector.

6.  Spring force ratios  
   – PT/P  
     • Ratio of the transversal force (PT) to the main axial force (P).  
   – DP/P  
     • Defined as (P1 – P2) / [(P1 + P2)/2], i.e. the normalized difference between two parallel spring forces.

How these TYPE codes are used in context:  
• In a HIST input record, up to 32 TYPE literals may be listed to request the time history of those variables.  
• The system will automatically compute and report the maximum and minimum of each selected curve.  
• Values are saved to the database for interactive post-processing (e.g. DYNR), printed directly, or dumped to an external file.  
• For beam-type elements and sectional stresses, auxiliary input fields XREF and INC further control where along the beam length (XREF) and at which stress-point location (INC) the values are evaluated. Negative XREF values specify a ratio of position to total length (e.g. –1.0 = beam end). An INC of zero requests only between FROM and TO time steps; INC > 0 triggers a relative change to prestressing force or a search for a matching rotational spring to compute ΔP from bending moment and plan-view distances.

Cross-references (“See also”)  
ECHO, CTRL, GRP, MASS, EIGE, MODD, STEP, LC, CONT, EXTR  
• These control other aspects of analysis setup, output control, grouping, mass properties, eigenvalue computations, modal damping, solution steps, load case management, continuation methods and modal extraction routines.  
• In combination with HIST and TYPE, they form the complete picture of how a user specifies, computes and extracts dynamic and static results in the solver environment.

By capturing each TYPE literal, its group (kinematic, dynamic, spring-force related) and its precise definition, a RAG vector store can deliver very accurate, targeted retrieval: e.g. “Show me all spring-force ratios” → fetch PT/P and DP/P; or “List all translational kinematics” → UX, UY, UZ, VX, VY, VZ, AX, AY, AZ.

The table in question is part of the HIST input-record definition (see “See also: ECHO, CTRL, GRP, MASS, EIGE, MODD, STEP, LC, CONT, EXTR”) and specifically enumerates the values you can request for time-history output.  Up to 32 such requests can be made in one HIST record.  The solver will automatically track and record the requested quantities between the time steps FROM…TO (with INC controlling the output increment), compute their time‐history envelopes (max/min), and either store them for DYNR presentation or dump them directly to a file.

Below is a breakdown of each code (the TYP field in HIST) and its meaning.  Whenever relevant, additional context from the HIST record description is noted (for example, how beam results use XREF to locate a section and INC to select a stress point).

1. Sum of all spring force components  
   • Resultant magnitude of all force components in a single spring element (P = √(Px²+Py²+Pz²+…)).  

2. Sum of the spring force components  
   • Vector sum of each individual force component (Px+Py+Pz).  

3. Sum of the spring moment components  
   • Scalar sum of the spring’s moment components about the global axes (Mx+My+Mz).  

4. Scalar axial force  
   • Axial (normal) force in the spring or bar element—i.e. the component along the element axis.  

5. Vector axial force  
   • The axial force expressed as a signed vector quantity (including sign sense).  

6. Beam forces  
   • Combined set of internal beam forces (axial plus shear) evaluated at a section.  Use XREF to define the section location:  
     – XREF>0: absolute distance from element start.  
     – XREF<0: ratio to total beam length (–1.0 → beam end).  

7. Beam forces normal and shear  
   • Splits the beam’s internal force into normal (axial) and shear components at the chosen section.  

8. Beam moments torsion and bending  
   • Torsional moment plus the bending moments about the local section axes.  

9. Stresses in sectional points  
   • Nodal or integration‐point stresses at a beam section.  INC selects which stress point (SPT) to evaluate; INC=0 suppresses this outside the FROM…TO range.  

10. All forces  
   • Complete set of force resultants for the element (including axial, shear, membrane, etc.) in one output vector.  

11. All moments  
   • All moment resultants (bending, torsion, membrane moment in shells, etc.) at the section.  

12. All shear forces  
   • Full vector of shear forces only (excludes axial).  

13. Membrane forces  
   • In shell or continuum elements, the in‐plane membrane force resultants (Nx, Ny, Nxy).  

14. Continua stresses  
   • Stress components in solid (3D continuum) elements—σxx, σyy, σzz, τxy, τyz, τzx.  

15. Volumes of 3D continuum  
   • Integrated volume or volume‐weighted result over a solid element or group of elements.  

16. Stresses of 3D continuum  
   • Equivalent or principal stresses (e.g. von Mises) computed for solid elements.  

17. Impedance of translatoric degrees of freedom  
   • Frequency‐analysis output: the complex translational stiffness (real and imaginary parts) of a node or set of nodes.  

18. Impedance of rotational degrees of freedom  
   • Frequency‐analysis output: the complex rotational stiffness for a given node or pair of nodes.  

Additional notes:  
• For spring-force ratios you can also request:  
   – PT/P = transverse (lateral) force PT divided by main spring force P.  
   – DP/P = (P₁−P₂)/( (P₁+P₂)/2 ), i.e. normalized force difference between two parallel springs.  
• If INC > 0 and the element is prestressed, the HIST output will report ΔP (change relative to prestress) instead of absolute P.  The code hunts for a “rotational spring” on the same nodes to derive ΔP from the moment and plan‐view distance (using XREF…ZREF to locate points).  
• The solver always prints the computed maximum and minimum of each requested quantity over the entire time range, even if you opt to dump only instantaneous values.  
• HIST values can be viewed later with “DYNR” (for interactive plotting) or can be sent to an external file for post-processing.

See also: ECHO, CTRL, GRP, MASS, EIGE, MODD, STEP, LC, CONT, EXTR

Below is a field-by-field breakdown of the input table that governs the extraction and storage of maximum/minimum structural results in a RAG-style vector database. Wherever useful, cross-references to the extended context are noted.

1. General Behavior  
   • Two storage modes exist for extreme results:  
     – “First option” (bold TYPE literals, default “!”) captures only individual extreme values (no accompanying force sets). These records cannot be meaningfully superposed.  
     – “Second option” (all other TYPE literals) pairs each extreme key value with its full set of corresponding forces.  

2. Item: TYPE  
   • Description: Selects which structural magnitude or result category to process. Possible literals include standard result types such as ECHO, CTRL, GRP, MASS, EIGE, MODD, STEP, LC, CONT, HIST, EXTR, etc.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal)  
   • Default: “!” (implies the first option—store only extreme scalars).  
   • Notes:  
     – If you need full force vectors with your extremes (second option), choose a non-bold TYPE.  
     – Bold types are limited to isolated extremes and cannot participate in statistical or steady-state superposition.  

3. Item: MAX  
   • Description: Load-case number whose results define the maximum extreme.  
   • Unit: – (not applicable)  
   • Default: 0  
   • Notes:  
     – A zero value means “print only,” with no storage of MAX.  
     – To record maximum nodal displacements (U, V), velocities (VELO), or accelerations (ACCE), supply a non-zero case number and use ECHO DISP/VELO/ACCE.  

4. Item: MIN  
   • Description: Load-case number whose results define the minimum extreme.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 0  
   • Notes:  
     – Like MAX, 0 yields print-only. Supplying a case >0 instructs the database to store the minimum.  

5. Item: STYP  
   • Description: Statistical or steady-state superposition method for combining multiple cases.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: *1 (follow CTRL STYP V2 settings)  
   • Supported methods:  
     – ADD: Linear sum of values  
     – SUM: Sum of absolute values  
     – SRSS: Square root of sum of squares  
     – CQC: Complete Quadratic Combination (default in SOFiSTiK, generally most reliable)  
   • Notes & Advanced Usage:  
     – SUM, SRSS, CQC yield always-positive results even if individual contributions are negative.  
     – For single-item superposition across eigenforms, SOFiSTiK’s proprietary algorithm assembles full signed sets (leading term forced positive). External sign multipliers may be required in downstream tasks.  
     – Spectral wind loads: combine mean ± turbulent parts via MPLC/APLC/SPLC/RPLC flags on VAL; mean wind case passed in V3.  
     – To enforce “always unfavourable” sign based on a reference case, set CTRL STYP V3.  

6. Item: ACT  
   • Description: Assigns the result set to a named action (as defined in SOFiLOAD’s ACT records), facilitating later superposition.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: – (no action assigned)  

By configuring these five fields, users can precisely control which extremes are evaluated, how they’re combined, and how they’re catalogued in the vector store for efficient retrieval and post-processing.
