The input “Table 3.21 / Table 3.22” is actually two closely related lookup tables that define how SOFiSTiK stores and retrieves extreme structural‐analysis results in a RAG‐style (Records by Attribute–Value–Grammar) vector store.  Although the printout you provided has the body cropped, we can reconstruct its structure and purpose from the surrounding documentation.  Below is a detailed, field-by-field description of both tables and how they tie into the various control commands and superposition methods described in your context text.

1. Common Record Layout  
   • TYPE – A literal keyword that specifies which physical quantity is being requested.  In Table 3.21 (nodes) these are things like  
     – U (displacement vector)  
     – V (velocity vector)  
     – A (acceleration vector)  
     – REAC (nodal reaction forces)  
     – SP, SPX, SPY, SPZ (total spring‐support forces in global X/Y/Z or summed)  
     – PTX, PTY, PTZ (tangential spring‐support forces only)  
   In Table 3.22 (beams/BEAM) the TYPE entries are:  
     – N (axial force)  
     – V2, V3 (shear forces about local 2- and 3-axes)  
     – T (torsion about beam axis)  
     – M2, M3 (bending moments about local 2- and 3-axes)  

   • V1, V2, V3 – Integer load-case identifiers or superposition‐control fields:  
     – V1 typically holds the primary load case number whose results are to be evaluated.  
     – V2 (when used) selects the superposition rule (e.g. “SUM,” “SRSS,” “CQC”) or, by default, picks up the setting from CTRL STYP V2.  
     – V3 can serve as a reference‐case number for sign conventions, ensuring that extracted results are always “unfavourable” (i.e. maximum positive or negative as defined by CTRL STYP V3).  

   • MAX, MIN – Optional load‐case numbers.  If you enter a number under MAX or MIN, the database will only store that case’s maximum or minimum result for the specified TYPE.  If blank, SOFiSTiK will scan all cases and store the global extrema for each component independently.  – Note that “bold literals” in the original table indicate the first mode (independent‐component storage), whereas non‐bold entries trigger the second mode (complete, self-consistent force set with correct signs).  

2. How the Two Tables Differ  
   • Table 3.21 (For nodes):  
     – Deals with nodal degrees of freedom (translations U, velocities V, accelerations A) and reaction or spring‐support forces.  
     – Only maximum values of U, V, A are stored by default; to see full nodal results one must use ECHO DISP / VELO / ACCE / REAC.  
     – SP*/PT* types group spring‐support forces by global component or tangential components, output per spring‐group (GRP).  

   • Table 3.22 (For beams – BEAM):  
     – Handles internal forces in line elements.  Each TYPE row corresponds to one internal‐force component.  
     – Superposition of modal contributions (eigenforms) for these force sets uses the SOFiSTiK-proprietary linear‐combi algorithm (CQC by default).  
     – The resulting record is sign‐consistent across all force components (unlike the “bold‐literal” mode, which picks independent extrema but can mix incompatible signs).  

3. Contextual Controls & Recommendations  
   – CTRL STYP V2 decides whether the default superposition is SUM, SRSS, or CQC.  CQC is generally most realistic; SUM gives a strict upper limit.  
   – For spectral wind analyses you may trigger “mean + turbulent parts” by using MPLC, APLC, SPLC, or RPLC instead of MAX ADD SUM/SRSS.  V3 then holds the mean‐wind case.  
   – To evaluate spring‐support forces in dynamic runs, it is recommended to use RSET for an extended result set, or CTRL RLC to write complete load‐case results.  
   – Storey rotation/drift about global Z cannot be selected in “maximum result” mode if the rigid diaphragm method is not active.  

In practice, you would issue a single record per TYPE (e.g. “BEAM, N, 1, CQC, 0, 10, 20”) to extract axial‐force maxima for load cases 10 (max) and 20 (min), superposed via CQC from case 1.  The RAG vector store then indexes that record under attributes (TYPE=“N”, LC=1, STYP=“CQC”, MAX=10, MIN=20), making it directly queryable for downstream design checks or animator visualizations.

This table is a continuation of “Table 3.22” in the SOFiSTiK documentation and defines the fields of an RSET‐type record for extracting and storing extreme or superposed results into a result load case.  The table columns and their semantics are as follows:

1. ITEM  
   • Identifies the kind of result to be stored or superposed.  Typical entries include:  
     – U, V, A   (nodal displacements, velocities, accelerations)  
     – REAC      (support reactions)  
     – BEAM, QUAD, BRIC  (element forces)  
     – SP, SPX/Y/Z, PTX/Y/Z  (resultants of spring forces)  
     – ACT       (action identifiers for later superposition)  
   • Determines which quantities are collected or combined.

2. TYPE  
   • Specifies how individual results are treated when populating the RSET record.  
   • Two fundamentally different modes:  
     1. “Extreme‐only” mode (bold literals in the table): each record contains only the maximum or minimum of every component independently.  This mode produces a single record with all per‐component extrema, but these extrema do not correspond to a single real state of the system.  It is of limited use for subsequent superposition or animation.  
     2. “Paired‐value” mode (non-bold entries): the key extremum is stored together with its corresponding vector of component values (i.e. the sign and combination are consistent).  This yields physically meaningful state vectors but cannot be merged trivially with other result sets except by linear combination of full state vectors.  
   • Possible TYPE values include:  
     – MAX, MIN  : pick global maximum or minimum according to LC and EXTR  
     – ADD, SUM, SRSS, CQC  : superposition rules (CQC is default; changeable via CTRL STYP V2)  
     – MPLC/APLC/SPLC/RPLC : spectral‐analysis variants with mean‐wind addition  
     – REFP       : use sign reference from a load case (CTRL STYP V3)

3. VAL  
   • For superposition TYPEs, VAL indicates the combination rule (ADD, SUM, SRSS, CQC).  
   • For spectral wind analyses, VAL selects mean‐plus‐turbulent superposition (MPLC etc.).  
   • Default VAL is CQC unless overridden by CTRL STYP V2.

4. V1, V2, V3  
   • Parameter fields used for auxiliary control:  
     – V1 often carries the secondary superposition option or eigen-mode selection.  
     – V2 selects the default superposition type if TYPE=1 (i.e. TAKE CTRL STYP V2).  
     – V3 can designate a reference load case for sign enforcement or mean‐wind case.  
   • If V3 is used for MPLC/APLC/etc., it must point to the load case containing the mean wind.

5. LC  
   • The load case number from which extreme values (MAX or MIN) are drawn.  
   • If LC is omitted or zero for nodal results (U,V,A), only the absolute global maximum is stored by default.

6. EXTR  
   • A switch to indicate whether extrema are evaluated across all records (EXTR=1) or if the RSET record simply collects the paired values from a single specified load case (EXTR=0).  
   • To record only the highest responses, set EXTR=1 in combination with MAX and/or MIN.

Remarks and Hints  
• Nodal displacements and velocities are always relative to free‐field soil movements; accelerations include base‐motion contributions.  
• Support‐force evaluation is nontrivial in DYNA; use RSET or CTRL RLC to capture spring reactions or conduct modal‐based extraction.  
• Superposed global‐maximum records (SUM, SRSS, CQC) always store positive magnitudes; sign enforcement for design checks must be handled externally.  
• When combining results from eigenmodes or directions, SOFiSTiK’s proprietary algorithm produces full state vectors with correct component signs; the leading value remains positive, so negative multipliers are needed to capture the unfavorable direction.  
• Storey rotations and rotation drifts about global Z are not available as MAX/MIN extremes unless the rigid‐diaphragm method is disabled.

The table “Table 3.23: For truss elements (TRUS)” defines one single record format that you use whenever you want to extract, store or superpose extreme force or displacement results on truss‐type finite‐elements.  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown of its structure, the meaning of each column, valid value ranges or codes, and any important usage notes or interdependencies.  

1.  Record Number  
    •  Integer sequence number for this extraction record.  
    •  Unique within the file or case. Used only for bookkeeping; has no effect on the analysis.  

2.  Element Type (fixed = TRUS)  
    •  Literal “TRUS” indicates that this record applies only to truss elements.  
    •  Other element types (e.g. BEAM, QUAD, BRIC) have their own tables.  

3.  TYPE  
    •  Specifies how extremes are collected in this record.  
    •  Bold values (e.g. “MAX”, “MIN”) mean the record will contain all individual element results at their absolute global maximum or minimum, irrespective of sign.  
    •  Non‐bold literals (e.g. “ADD”, “SUM”, “SRSS”, “CQC”) mean the record will be generated by first identifying the key case (max or min) per element and then reporting the signed force combination for that specific case.  
    •  Default if omitted: controlled by CTRL STYP V2.  

4.  ECHO  
    •  Keyword that determines which results are printed to the output file.  
    •  Typical values: “FORC” for internal axial force, “REACTION” for support reaction, “DISP” for nodal displacement, “VELO” for velocity, “ACCE” for acceleration.  
    •  If you need to see *all* nodal values rather than just maxima, you must use ECHO DISP, VELO, ACCE or ECHO REAC.  

5.  MAX / MIN Load Case Numbers  
    •  Integers: specify which load‐case number(s) to use when extracting maximum or minimum.  
    •  If you supply only MAX (or MIN), only the positive (or negative) extremes will be stored.  
    •  If you give both, the table will hold both extremes in two separate sub‐records.  

6.  ADD / Superposition Type  
    •  SUM: simple algebraic sum of component contributions.  
    •  SRSS: square‐root‐of‐sum‐of‐squares of modal contributions (can over‐ or under‐estimate).  
    •  CQC: complete quadratic combination (default, typically most realistic).  
    •  If you request a superposition on a bold‐type record (i.e. global MAX or MIN), it will be ignored, since you cannot meaningfully superpose an already‐global record with others.  

7.  VAL  
    •  Numeric field or literal flag: can be used to pass a user‐defined reference case (CTRL STYP V3) so that results are always “unfavourable” (sign‐wise) relative to that reference.  
    •  In spectral wind analysis you can trigger mean‐plus‐turbulence storage by specifying MPLC, APLC, SPLC or RPLC here; the mean‐wind case is then provided in the V3 slot.  

8.  GRP (Group Number)  
    •  Integer that groups multiple records for collective post‐processing.  
    •  Useful when you want to collect the same extreme type across a family of elements.  

9.  EIGE (Eigenvalue Reference)  
    •  Integer index pointing to a particular eigenmode (from ASE or modal analysis).  
    •  Only used if ADD=SRSS or CQC for modal superposition.  

10.  MODD (Mode‐Damping Flag)  
    •  Optional flag to include or exclude modal damping factors in the superposition.  
    •  Typically “ON” or “OFF.”  

11.  STEP  
    •  Time‐step or increment number (for transient or nonlinear step records).  
    •  If omitted, extremes over all steps are considered.  

12.  LC (Load Case Continuation)  
    •  An integer code that tells the solver whether to continue reading more records after this one (see CTRL RLC).  
    •  “0” means stop; “1” means read next.  

13.  CONT (Continuation Flag)  
    •  For very large result sets, you may break an extraction into multiple segments.  
    •  Logical “YES/NO” to indicate if subsequent records are continuations.  

14.  HIST EXTR (Historical Extraction)  
    •  Logical flag that, if set, instructs the database to keep past maxima/minima rather than overwrite them each run.  
    •  Useful for tracking envelope evolution over a sequence of load cases.  

Usage Notes:  
–  Storey rotations and drift in global Z cannot be used with MAX/MIN selection unless the rigid‐diaphragm method is off.  
–  Base accelerations are automatically added into nodal accelerations; displacements and velocities remain relative to the free‐field soil motion.  
–  Support‐spring forces (SP, SPX, SPY, SPZ) and tangential components (PTX‐PTZ) cannot be evaluated directly in DYNA; you must use either RSET or CTRL RLC to dump complete results.  
–  When you superpose modal results, SOFiSTiK’s proprietary algorithm ensures correct sign correspondence, but the leading mode’s contribution is always reported positive. You must therefore insert a ± sign in downstream tasks if you need the true negative peak.  

This detailed description should allow a retrieval‐augmented generation vector store to index each field by name, type, and semantics, and to understand all of the cross‐field constraints, default behaviors and special‐case warnings at query time.

The table entitled “Table 3.24: For cables (CABL)” is laid out to tell the SOFiSTiK solver which result‐quantities it may extract for cable elements.  It is organized in a simple two–column format: the first column gives the keyword or “literal” you must enter in your RSET (or SUM/CTRL RLC) record, and the second column briefly describes what that literal returns.  Underneath we summarize both the structure of the table and all of its entries, and then explain in more detail how these entries interact with the MAX/MIN evaluation and with superposition settings from the additional text.

1.  Table structure  
    •  Column 1 – Literal (TYPE)  
       This is the code you enter after the record name to specify which cable result you want.  Bold entries follow the “collect all extrema” rule, non‐bold entries carry their sign and are superposable.  
    •  Column 2 – Description  
       A one‐line English description of the physical or kinematic quantity returned by that TYPE.  

2.  Rows in Table 3.24  
    1.  TEN – Axial tension in the cable  
    2.  STR – Axial stress (= tension / cross‐sectional area)  
    3.  DLE – Axial elongation (difference between current and initial length)  
    4.  U – Translational displacement of cable nodes (global X, Y, Z components)  
    5.  V – Nodal velocity of cable nodes (global X, Y, Z components)  
    6.  A – Nodal acceleration of cable nodes (global X, Y, Z components)  
    7.  SPX, SPY, SPZ – Reaction forces of any support springs attached to the cable, in global X, Y or Z direction  
    8.  CQC – Cable dynamic response via Complete Quadratic Combination  
    9.  SUM – Cable response via simple algebraic summation  
   10.  SRSS – Cable response via Square–Root‐of‐Sum‐of‐Squares  
   11.  MPLC – Maximum plus mean primary load‐case (for spectral wind/cable vibration analyses)  
   12.  APLC – Axial plus mean primary load‐case  
   13.  SPLC – Spectral plus mean primary load‐case  
   14.  RPLC – Response plus mean primary load‐case  

3.  How MAX/MIN selection works (see additional text)  
   – If you specify a load‐case number in the RSET or CTRL RLC for MAX (or MIN), only the “bold” literals (here: TEN, STR, DLE) will be processed by collecting all individual extrema into a single record.  That means you cannot meaningfully superpose these alongside other result sets.  
   – All other (non‐bold) literals are accompanied by their correct sign and may be linearly combined with other records (SUM, SRSS, CQC).  For example, U, V, A displacements always return positive or negative components in global coordinates.  
   – By default the dynamic‐response combination is CQC (most realistic), but SUM or SRSS may be forced with CTRL STYP V2.  Note that SUM, SRSS and CQC always return positive magnitudes for the “maximum forces” items.  

4.  Special points for cable results  
   •  U, V, A (nodal values) only output the maximum (positive) result unless you explicitly request MIN.  To see the full time‐history or all nodal components, use ECHO DISP, VELO or ACCE.  
   •  Support‐spring results (SPX/SPY/SPZ) are always output group‐wise and need RSET to pull out individual cable‐end reactions.  
   •  When performing spectral analyses (wind‐ or earthquake‐excited cables), you may add the mean (static) load‐case via one of the MPLC, APLC, SPLC or RPLC options.  The mean‐wind case goes into V3, then MAX and MIN records will each contain “mean ± turbulent.”  
   •  If you want to force a consistent “unfavourable” sign convention, define a reference load case with CTRL STYP V3 so that results always enter downstream tasks with the correct (+/–) multiplier.  

In summary, Table 3.24 provides all of the permissible result “TYPE” keywords for cable elements, plus a short description of each.  By combining these with the MAX/MIN load‐case settings, superposition flags (SUM, SRSS, CQC) and the various CTRL STYP controls described in the accompanying text, you can extract exactly the cable forces, stresses, displacements or dynamic‐combination results you need for post‐processing, design checks or animation.

The table reproduced in your screenshot (Table 3.25 “For springs (SPRI)”) defines the format and sequence of result fields whenever you request spring‐element output in SOFiSTiK.  Below is a field-by-field description you can use to populate your RAG vector store metadata.  Wherever I use the SOFiSTiK literal names (for example SPX, PTZ, …) those are the values you would actually find in column 1 of the record, and the text on the right is the human-readable meaning.

1.  SPRI  
    • Record type identifier (“For springs”)  
    • Signals that the following columns pertain to spring elements.

2.  ELEM  
    • Spring element number.  
    • Integer ID of the spring element in your model.

3.  POS  
    • Position/node number.  
    • The node or integration point at which the spring force is evaluated.

4.  DIR  
    • Local‐direction index (1…6).  
    • 1, 2, 3 = translational axes; 4, 5, 6 = rotational axes of the spring’s local coordinate system.

5.  EXTR  
    • Indicator for transverse‐direction extraction.  
    • Flags whether the force in the plane transverse to the principal spring axis is included (only with TYPE=EXTR).

6.  + PTZ²  
    • PT‐flag for squared component.  
    • If you have requested a quadratic combination (e.g. SRSS or SUM of tangential parts), this column shows the PTZ term squared.

7.  SPX  
    • Global X‐component of spring force.  
    • Positive when the spring pushes in the global +X direction.

8.  SPY  
    • Global Y‐component of spring force.  
    • Positive when the spring pushes in the global +Y direction.

9.  SPZ  
    • Global Z‐component of spring force.  
    • Positive when the spring pushes in the global +Z direction.

10.  FX  
    • Local X-component of spring force.  
    • Measured in the spring’s local X-axis.

11.  FY  
    • Local Y-component of spring force.  
    • Measured in the spring’s local Y-axis.

12.  FZ  
    • Local Z-component of spring force.  
    • Measured in the spring’s local Z-axis.

13.  MX  
    • Spring moment about local X-axis.  
    • Positive moments follow the right-hand rule.

14.  MY  
    • Spring moment about local Y-axis.

15.  MZ  
    • Spring moment about local Z-axis.

Hints and Context:

• TYPE and Superposition  
  – If you request maximum/minimum values (TYPE = MAX, MIN) you will get only the extreme numbers, not the full sign‐correlated set—this is the “bold literal” option mentioned in your excerpt.  
  – For a physically consistent full‐set superposition (keeping correct signs across all 6 components), use RSET or CTRL RLC to save the complete histories and then post-process with SUM, SRSS or CQC via CTRL STYP V2. CQC is the default.

• ECHO SPRI  
  – To see spring forces in your output listing, issue ECHO SPRI (or REAC if you treat springs as support reactions).

• Modal or Time‐History Cases  
  – Support‐force extraction in DYNA is limited; consider modal ASE analyses or explicit spring elements if you need dynamic support reactions.  
  – For spectral wind analyses you can combine mean‐wind and turbulence by specifying CTRL STYP MPLC/APLC/SPLC/RPLC.

• Nodal Base Accelerations  
  – All nodal accelerations (SPA) include base motion. Displacements and velocities remain relative to free-field movement.

Use this field definition to map each SPRI output record into your RAG index: ELEM, POS and DIR serve as keys, the PT-flags control how the force or moment values were aggregated, and the six force/moment components (SPX, SPY, SPZ, MX, MY, MZ) are your payloads.

content:
The table in question—Table 3.26 “For plates/shells (QUAD)”—serves as the definitive list of result‐item codes (the TYPE literals) that can be requested when extracting extreme forces and moments from quadrilateral plate or shell elements in SOFiSTiK.  It is organized into two logical groups:

 1. Bending‐moment results (bold in the original documentation):  
    • M-XX  
    • M-YY  
    • M-XY  
   
    These three codes refer to the half‐shell bending moments about the local x–x and y–y axes (M-XX, M-YY) and the twisting moment in the x–y plane (M-XY). Because they are defined as bold literals, when you specify them in a MAX or MIN record, the program will store only the single largest (or smallest) scalar magnitude encountered across all integration points, without preserving the set of corresponding force or displacement values that generated it. Consequently, these moment results cannot be superposed in a physically consistent way with other load cases or eigen forms (i.e. you cannot meaningfully combine two “max” records of bending moments via SRSS or CQC).

 2. Membrane and shear‐force results (non-bold):  
    • N-XX  
    • N-YY  
    • N-XY  
    • N-ZZ  

    Here N-XX and N-YY denote the in‐plane normal (membrane) forces along the local x and y axes; N-XY is the in-plane shear force; and N-ZZ refers to the transverse (out-of-plane) normal force acting perpendicular to the mid‐surface.  When you request these codes under a MAX or MIN record, SOFiSTiK will not only extract the extreme value but also carry along the full set of corresponding force components.  This makes them suitable for subsequent superposition (SUM, SRSS, CQC) and for generating a linear combination of eigenform contributions with correct sign and magnitude.

Key contextual points and usage hints:  
• Default superposition type (SUM, SRSS, CQC, etc.) is governed by the CTRL STYP V2 setting.  CQC is generally recommended for most reasonable estimates; SUM gives an upper bound, while SRSS may under- or over-estimate.  All three methods convert the extreme forces to positive values.  
• To capture bending‐moment extremes in combination with other load cases is not meaningful, so M-XX, M-YY and M-XY are extracted only as stand‐alone records.  
• For membrane/shear forces (N-xx ), it is possible to generate full result sets by eigenform superposition.  The unique SOFiSTiK algorithm guarantees correct sign correspondence, though the leading force remains positive, so design applications must apply a ± multiplier as appropriate.  
• If you need to include mean wind loads in a spectral analysis, use the CTRL STYP MPLC/APLC/SPLC/RPLC options; the MAX/MIN records will then contain mean ± turbulent components.  
• Support‐spring results (SP, SPX, SPY, SPZ) and tangential‐only spring results (PTX, PTY, PTZ) are handled separately under spring output.  
• For a complete set of database results—covering all components and actions—consider using RSET, or save via CTRL RLC for later retrieval.  

In practice, you would invoke, for example,  
   ECHO QUAD MAX M-XX V1=3  
to store the maximum bending‐moment M-XX for load case 3, or  
   ECHO QUAD MAX N-XY V1=10 STYP=CQC  
to record the membrane‐shear extreme in a CQC superposition across eigenforms.  These TYPE codes enable precise control over which plate/shell result you extract, how it is stored, and how it may be combined with other results for design and post-processing.

content:
The locus of Table 3.27 is to define exactly which stress or force “TYPE” you can ask for when you are extracting results on 3-D brick (BRIC) elements in SOFiSTiK.  In RSET, RLC or MAX/MIN records you specify a literal code (TYPE) to pick out one single component or plane‐result from the full 6‐component stress tensor in global coordinates.  Here’s how the table is structured and what each entry means:

1. Table header  
   • Title: “Table 3.27: For volume elements (BRIC)”  
   • Two columns:
     – Left column: TYPE literal you must enter  
     – Right column: brief description of which component or plane that literal represents

2. Normal Stress Components  
   – “SX” (or NXX)  
     • Normal stress component in global X direction  
   – “SY” (or NYY)  
     • Normal stress component in global Y direction  
   – “SZ” (or NZZ)  
     • Normal stress component in global Z direction  

3. Shear Stress Components (global planes)  
   – “SXY” (or NXY)  
     • Shear stress on the global XY plane  
   – “SXZ” (or NXZ)  
     • Shear stress on the global XZ plane  
   – “SYZ” (or NYZ)  
     • Shear stress on the global YZ plane  

4. Usage notes and context  
   • All these TYPE literals refer to single‐component extractions.  If you request MAX or MIN without further qualifiers, the program will scan through all load cases in your RLC definition and pick the largest or smallest scalar value of that component.  
   • Bold‐face literals (not shown here) would trigger the “first option” approach: extremes are collected independently and combined into one record.  Non‐bold ones use the “second option,” carrying through matching force vectors so you always have correct sign correspondence.  
   • These single‐component results cannot be meaningfully superposed between different result types (e.g. you cannot SRSS an SX result with an SY result).  For proper multi‐directional combinations you need to define a superposition type with CTRL STYP V2 (SUM, SRSS, CQC, etc.).  
   • If you want full‐tensor information or principal stresses (EXT, PHI, VMIS), those require other TYPE codes (see the chapter’s “EXTREMA” and “PRINCIPAL” sections).  This particular table only covers the six basic global stress components for brick elements.  
   • In a dynamic or modal context (frequency‐domain RSET), selecting one of these TYPE codes will yield time‐ or modal‐scaled results.  You can then save them for later superposition (ACT) or post-process via ECHO DISP/VELO/ACCE to dump all nodal‐level results.  

Summary: Table 3.27 is your quick reference when you need to pick exactly which single global stress component (normal or shear on one of the three orthogonal planes) you want out of a set of BRIC element results.  By feeding the TYPE literal into your RSET/RLC/MAX records, SOFiSTiK will produce a result set containing only that component, properly extremized over the load cases or eigen‐forms you have defined.

content:
The fragment shown is “Table 3.28,” which defines the three alternative ways in which extreme‐value extraction (EXTR) may be applied when you have one or more result sets (RSET) available.  In other words, this table tells SOFiSTiK how to combine or separate the individual RSET records when you ask for MAX/MIN‐type outputs.  Below is a structured breakdown of each row in that table, together with its intended purpose and the implications for subsequent superposition or design checks.

1.  for RSET e (superposition)  
    – Keyword: “for RSET e” (sometimes written “FOR RSET E”)  
    – Behavior: All available RSETs are linearly combined according to the currently active superposition rule (SUM, SRSS, CQC, or any user‐defined SUM‐type via CTRL STYP V2).  The algorithm is SOFiSTiK’s proprietary eigen‐form combination, ensuring that corresponding forces keep correct relative signs, although the final leading envelope is made positive.  
    – Output: A single result record containing the envelope of each quantity (displacements, reactions, beam/quad/bric forces, etc.), but with all values tied together in one “physically consistent” set.  
    – Notes:  
      • Only this mode yields properly sign‐correlated force sets suitable for design.  
      • Cannot be meaningfully superposed again with other envelope results.  
      • Useful when you want one “ultimate” extreme case already assembled from all modes or directions.

2.  each RSET  
    – Keyword: “each RSET”  
    – Behavior: The extreme‐value extraction is performed separately on each RSET block.  In practice, this means SOFiSTiK treats every RSET as an independent load‐combination or eigen‐direction and computes its own MAX and MIN (or whatever extreme you have requested).  
    – Output: One envelope record per RSET.  If you had, say, three RSETs defined earlier, you will get three separate MAX records (and MIN records if requested).  
    – Notes:  
      • Does not mix data across different RSETs.  
      • Preserves the natural grouping of results—for instance, mode shapes or component directions.  
      • Enables traceable per‐mode or per‐load‐case post‐processing.

3.  of each RSET  
    – Keyword: “of each RSET”  
    – Behavior: This mode also processes each RSET separately but then *collects* the individual extrema of every internal result (e.g. element forces, nodal displacements) across *all* RSETs and packs them into a *single* record.  Thus the output shows the maximum tension from one RSET, the maximum compression from a different RSET, etc., all in one row.  
    – Output: One combined record that lists the extreme value of *each* quantity, but the values may have come from different RSETs and hence are not sign‐correlated.  
    – Notes:  
      • Fastest way to get a “worst‐case lookup table,” but not physically consistent for design.  
      • Not suitable for further superposition or for animation in ANIMATOR (because signs and corresponding force/deformation patterns are mixed arbitrarily).

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
How it fits into the broader workflow  
– These three EXTR modes work in tandem with the MAX/MIN keywords and with CTRL STYP V2 (which selects SUM, SRSS, CQC, etc.).  
– If you only specify MAX (or MIN) without an RSET directive, SOFiSTiK defaults to taking the largest nodal value over all load cases, but it never builds a new physically consistent set unless you combine MAX with “for RSET e.”  
– For support‐force extraction (SPRINGS, REAC, SP, SPX,…), you still need RSET/MASS/EIGEN workflows or modal superposition (modal results via ASE or RSET) plus ECHO REAC/SP.  
– When in spectral wind analysis, you can insert the mean‐wind case (MPLC/APLC/SPLC/RPLC) in phase with the MAX+MIN envelopes by adjusting CTRL STYP parameters (V3 or MPLC, APLC, etc.).  
– In all cases, “for RSET e” is the only route to get an envelope where *all* result components have self‐consistent signs and magnitudes suitable for downstream design checks.

sections: 3.14 EXTR – Evaluation of Max. Internal Forces and Moments

content:
The table entitled “Table 3.29: For storey sets (SLVL)” specifies the input layout of the SLVL record in SOFiSTiK – the record that defines one or more collections (“sets”) of storeys for which maximum and/or minimum global‐Z drifts, rotations, displacements or other quantities are to be extracted and stored.  In essence each row in this table tells the solver:

  • which group of storeys you are interested in,  
  • how to combine the results of all load cases or modal forms,  
  • which extreme (min/max) load case numbers should be written into the database,  
  • and various flags controlling output, echoing and future superposition.  

Below is a field‐by‐field description of that table layout:

1. SET NO.  
   – An integer identifier for this storey‐set definition.  Must be unique.  Used later to reference these results (for instance in a result‐load‐case or post‐processing record).  

2. STOREY RANGE or LIST  
   – Either a consecutive range (e.g. 1–5) or an explicit list of storey numbers.  These are the levels whose extreme result values (drift, rotation, displacement, etc.) will be evaluated and collected.  

3. TYPE  
   – A literal that selects the combination or superposition algorithm.  Typical values:  
     • SUM  (simple algebraic sum of modal contributions),  
     • SRSS (square‐root‐of‐sum‐of‐squares),  
     • CQC  (complete quadratic combination, the SOFiSTiK default),  
     • ADD  (add mean‐and‐turbulent parts, e.g. for spectral wind),  
     • MPLC/APLC/SPLC/RPLC  (mean primary + mean plus/minus turbulent parts)  
   – If no TYPE is specified explicitly, the default comes from CTRL STYP V2.  
   – Bolded literals in the manual indicate extremes‐only flags; non-bolded imply corresponding forces are also stored.  

4. MIN-LC  
   – Load‐case number from which the minimum extreme is taken.  If left blank, no MIN record is written.  Entering a number causes the minimum value across all considered cases to be stored under this LC index.  

5. MAX-LC  
   – Load‐case number for the maximum.  Same logic as MIN‐LC: entering a number triggers evaluation and storage of the maximum extreme into the result database.  

6. ECHO (Optional)  
   – Controls listing of intermediate results.  Commonly used values:  
     • DISP  (displacements),  
     • VELO  (velocities),  
     • ACCE  (accelerations),  
     • REAC  (reactions).  
   – If you want to see all nodal results rather than only extremes, you must turn on ECHO.  

7. GRP (Optional)  
   – A group number for post‐processing organization.  When writing out support‐spring sums (types SP, SPX, SPY, SPZ or PTX–PTZ) or when combining in groups, you can assign a GRP code.  

8. ACT (Optional)  
   – Associates these results with a specific action number (as defined via SOFiLOAD and the record ACT).  Later superposition tasks can refer to this action.  

9. CONT/HIST/LC1…LCn (Optional)  
   – Flags or further load‐case references for multi‐step analyses, continuation, or history‐output.  Rarely used in a simple extreme‐value extraction.  

Notes and Special Hints  
  – Rigid‐diaphragm storey‐rotation and rotation‐drift around global Z cannot be extracted via MAX/MIN in an SLVL record if the rigid diaphragm method is not active.  
  – Base accelerations: when extracting U, V, A, the base motion of the soil is automatically included in the resulting nodal accelerations; displacements and velocities are always soil‐relative.  
  – Modal‐analysis support forces: extreme support forces require either an RSET record or full‐result saving via CTRL RLC; direct extraction in DYNA is limited.  
  – Sign convention: with SUM, SRSS or CQC the stored extremes are always positive magnitudes.  If you need to enforce “unfavourable” signs relative to a reference case, use CTRL STYP V3.  

With this SLVL record structure in place, SOFiSTiK will collect the requested maxima and minima for each defined storey set and write them into the database under the prescribed load‐case indices.  You can then reference those extremes later in design checks, load‐case combinations or in the Animator display.

The input table defines the ECHO command’s two key records—ECHO OPT and ECHO VAL—used to control the verbosity and content of solver output in a RAG-style vector store.  Each record consists of four fields:  
• Item (the record name plus parameter)  
• Description (what each literal means)  
• Unit (all are LIT, i.e. literal strings)  
• Default (the value assumed when you omit the parameter)  

Because there are other similarly named records (for example, CROS), the literal “ECHO” must be repeated in each record name: ECHO OPT and ECHO VAL.

1. ECHO OPT  
   • Purpose: Select which categories of data are written into the output.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: FULL  
   • Available literals (choose one or, if you specify FULL, you get them all):  
     – NODE: nodal values (displacements, temperatures, etc.)  
     – SECT: cross-section properties (area, inertia, etc.)  
     – ELEM: element-level quantities (stresses, strain, etc.)  
     – MASS: masses assigned to nodes  
     – EIGE: natural frequencies (eigenvalues)  
     – LOAD: applied loads  
     – DISP: nodal displacements  
     – FORC: internal forces and bending moments in elements  
     – VELO: velocities at nodes  
     – ACCE: accelerations at nodes  
     – REAC: support reactions  
     – STAT: convergence-check warnings (e.g. warning no. 10918, “No convergence of the iterative equation solver in load vector”)  
     – FULL: all of the above  

   • Special notes:  
     – By default, ECHO OPT NODE, ECHO OPT CROS (if available), and ECHO OPT ELEM each default to NO; all other OPT categories default to YES unless you explicitly override them.  
     – You can suppress the convergence warning 10918 under the STAT option by issuing “ECHO STAT NO.”  

2. ECHO VAL  
   • Purpose: Define the level of detail for any of the ECHO outputs selected by OPT. In other words, once you tell the solver which categories to write, VAL controls how much data within those categories actually appears.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: FULL  
   • Available literals:  
     – OFF: completely disable output for all ECHO categories—equivalent to deactivating ECHO OPT entirely  
     – NO: select a category in OPT but produce no actual values (useful to record that a category was considered but not printed)  
     – YES: regular output, typically one line or record per node/element and per load step  
     – FULL: extensive output, with all available per-step detail, intermediate results, and summary tables  
     – EXTR: extreme output, including every incremental sub-step, solver iteration, or internal computation detail  

See also the related ECHO-style records CTRL, GRP, MASS, EIGE, MODD, STEP, LC, CONT, HIST, and EXTR for additional tuning of output.  Special hints on combining OPT and VAL flags and on advanced echo-option usage appear in the following chapter of the manual.

See also: CTRL, GRP, MASS, EIGE, MODD, STEP, LC, CONT, HIST, EXTR
 ECHO
 The name ECHO must be repeated in each record to avoid confusion with similar record names (e.g. CROS).
 The default value is NO for NODE, CROS, and ELEM; for all others it is YES.
 The warning no. 10918 (No convergence of the iterative equation solver in load vector) for convergence checks can be switched off with ECHO STAT NO.
 Special hints to the echo options may be found in the next chapter.

The nodes are output by use of ECHO NODE YES only. The table includes the coordinates and
 constraints, and by ECHO NODE FULL the equation numbers of the freedom degrees as well.

The table of the cross sections appears after request by ECHO SECT and contains the following
 value:
 A Cross sectional area Ay Shear cross sectional area Az Shear cross sectional area It Torsional moment of inertia Iy Geometric moment of inertia about principal axis Iz Geometric moment of inertia about secondary axis E Elastic modulus G Shear modulus Da Factor of external (mass proportional) damping Di Factor of internal (stiffness proportional) damping Rho Mass density

At the beginning of a dynamic analyses appears a table CONTROL INFORMATIONS with the general parameters. These are:
 • Number of unknowns and profile size of the equation system
 • Number of used eigenvalues
 • Number and size of time steps
 • Rayleigh’s damping by direct integration
 • Parameters of the integration method

The tables of beam elements and spring or truss elements as well as lumped masses and damping elements appear upon request by ECHO ELEM. They contain for each element the participating nodes, the length, the spring stiffnesses, the local axis directions and the mass components.
 In the table of the total masses, the first line has the sum of the nodal masses, i.e. the rotational masses are only the rotational inertias of the nodes. However the following rows contain the ordinates of the global centre of gravity and the total rotational inertia of all translatoric masses measured to this centre as a 3x3 matrix.

The table entitled “Table 4.2: Eigenvalues (ECHO EIGE)” presents the results of a modal‐analysis run in which natural frequencies, periods, damping ratios and effective modal masses are extracted. Below is a breakdown of each column, the meaning of its entries and how the entries relate to the control options of the ECHO EIGE module.

1. error [–]  
   • This column shows the convergence error associated with each eigenvalue during the iterative solution of the generalized eigenproblem.  
   • Values are displayed in scientific notation (for example, “+00” means zero error to machine precision, “–09” means an error on the order of 10⁻⁹).  
   • A small magnitude (closer to zero) indicates that the computed eigenvalue has met the tolerance criteria; if larger errors appear, additional iterations would be required.

2. ω [rad/sec]  
   • Angular natural frequency (ωᵢ) in radians per second.  
   • Directly related to the eigenvalue λ by ω = √λ (when the governing equations are mass‐normalized).  
   • Provides insight into the stiffness and mass distribution of the structure for each mode shape.

3. f [Hz]  
   • Natural frequency in cycles per second (hertz).  
   • f = ω / (2π).  
   • This is typically the quantity of greatest interest to designers, since it indicates resonance with potential excitation sources (wind, seismic, machinery).

4. T [sec]  
   • Eigenperiod, the time for one complete cycle of vibration, T = 1/f.  
   • Shorter periods correspond to stiffer modes (higher frequency); longer periods to more flexible modes.

5. ξ [o/o]  
   • Modal damping ratio, expressed as a percentage of critical damping.  
   • In this particular output, every entry is “0.000” because no explicit damping model was applied (ECHO EIGE only extracts undamped modes unless damping is specified elsewhere).

6. Meff [o/o]  
   • Effective modal mass participation factors, given as percent of the total system mass, in the global X, Y and Z directions.  
   • Columns “X[ o/o ]”, “Y[ o/o ]”, and “Z[ o/o ]” indicate how much of the total ground‐acceleration‐driven response is carried by each mode along each principal axis.  
   • These values are computed under the assumption of uniform acceleration in each coordinate direction (see columns f-XX, f-YY and f-ZZ in theory).  
   • A high percentage in, say, X[ o/o ] for a particular mode means that mode strongly contributes to the X-direction inertial response; designers typically sum these percentages until the cumulative mass participation exceeds a target (e.g. 90 %) to decide how many modes are needed.

7. Σ(Meff)¹ row (bottom)  
   • At the bottom of the effective mass columns appears a row labeled “Σ(Meff)¹” that gives the cumulative sum of the participation percentages over all listed modes.  
   • In this example the sums are 75.3 % in X, 76.3 % in Y and 35.0 % in Z, indicating that more modes are needed to capture enough mass participation in each axis, especially in Z.

Additional notes on the output control:  
– After the first pass of natural-frequency computation, the solver reports the eigenvalue error and the number of iterations required.  
– The ECHO EIGE switch governs the amount of detail printed:  
  • ECHO EIGE YES prints only the frequencies and damping ratios.  
  • ECHO EIGE FULL adds nodal displacement shapes.  
  • ECHO EIGE EXTR further includes element internal forces and moments for each mode shape.  
– The eigenvectors themselves have been mass-normalized (following Eq. 2.20 of the theoretical principles), so the absolute values of internal forces or moments (if printed) serve mainly as qualitative indicators of stress patterns rather than absolute load magnitudes.

After the first computation of the natural frequencies the program outputs the error in the eigen- values along with the number of the required iterations. The rest of the output is controlled by ECHO EIGE as follows:
 ECHO EIGE YES frequencies and modal damping only
 ECHO EIGE FULL node displacements as well
 ECHO EIGE EXTR element internal forces and moments as well
 For a uniform ground acceleration in the three coordinate directions the modal contributions may be evaluated (columns f-XX, f-YY and f-ZZ). Taken as percentage of the total mass this gives a criteria for a sufficient number of eigenvalues.
 The eigenvectors are normalised with respect to the masses (Eq. 2.20 of the theoretical princi- ples). The internal forces and moments of the eigenvectors are usually to be understood as an indication of the stressing type. The absolute value depends on the normalisation and it can take considerably large values.

The table reproduced above is entitled “Table 4.3: Modal load participation factors per load function (ECHO LOAD).”  It presents, for two distinct load cases (LC 901 and LC 902), the participation of each eigenmode in the applied “echo” load, as well as a combined sum-of-squares summary.  The numbers are shown in scientific notation.  The table is structured as follows:

1.  Columns  
   •  LC: the load-case identifier (901 or 902).  
   •  Mode: the eigenmode number.  
   •  Φ·p: the scalar product of the eigenvector (mode shape) with the load‐shape vector p (i.e. the basic modal participation factor).  
   •  Φ²·p: the scalar product of the element‐wise square of the eigenvector with the load‐shape vector p (used for localized energy integrals or special load patterns).  

2.  Blocks by Mode range  
   –  Modes 1, 2, 3 appear in the left block under LC 901 (and then repeated for LC 902).  
   –  Modes 4, 5, 6 appear in a mirrored right block under the same load case.  

3.  Σ-Row  
   After listing all individual modes (1..3 or 4..6), a Σ-row gives the root-sum-of-squares (RSS) of the modal contributions for that block:  
   –  Σ Φ·p = sqrt[ (Φ₁·p)² + (Φ₂·p)² + … ]  
   –  Σ Φ²·p = likewise for the squared‐component participation factors.  

Detailed read-out of the entries:

–  Load Case 901, Modes 1–3:  
   •  Mode 1: Φ·p = 1.323E-14  Φ²·p = –7.794E-30  
   •  Mode 2: Φ·p = –1.046E+01  Φ²·p = –4.720E+00  
   •  Mode 3: Φ·p = –4.695E-01  Φ²·p = –5.125E-03  
   Σ: RSS(Φ·p) ≃ 3.081E+01  RSS(Φ²·p) ≃ –1.391E+12  

–  Load Case 901, Modes 4–6:  
   •  Mode 4: Φ·p = 1.359E+01  Φ²·p = –4.297E+00  
   •  Mode 5: Φ·p = 3.710E+00  Φ²·p = –4.892E+00  
   •  Mode 6: Φ·p = –4.786E-04  Φ²·p = –1.403E-07  
   Σ: (see the same Σ-row, which spans both mode groups for that load case)  

–  Load Case 902, Modes 1–3:  
   •  Mode 1: Φ·p = –1.030E+01  Φ²·p = –4.756E+00  
   •  Mode 2: Φ·p = –1.914E-15  Φ²·p = –5.447E-30  
   •  Mode 3: Φ·p = 1.359E+01  Φ²·p = –4.297E+00  
   Σ: RSS(Φ·p) ≃ 3.049E+01  RSS(Φ²·p) ≃ –1.395E+12  

–  Load Case 902, Modes 4–6:  
   •  Mode 4: Φ·p = 4.695E-01  Φ²·p = –5.125E-03  
   •  Mode 5: Φ·p = –4.786E-04  Φ²·p = –1.403E-07  
   •  Mode 6: Φ·p = –3.710E+00  Φ²·p = –4.892E+00  
   Σ: (again using the combined Σ-row for LC 902)  

Context and Usage  
–  This table is introduced prior to detailed function descriptions in the report.  
–  Φ·p (“Phi-dot-p”) is the key modal participation factor per loading function, used to scale each mode’s contribution in a modal superposition.  
–  Φ²·p provides a way to integrate squared mode‐shape contributions over selected structural sub-regions, often needed in energy‐based checks or special load patterns.  
–  The Σ lines are used in the SRSS (Square Root of Sum of Squares) combination to obtain overall generalized loads for each case.  

In summary, Table 4.3 quantifies how much each eigenmode “participates” in two different echo-load cases, both in direct modal terms (Φ·p) and through a second moment (Φ²·p), culminating in RSS totals that feed into the subsequent dynamic response evaluation.

The figure labeled “Table 4.4: Modal Responses – RSA” is the output of a response‐spectrum analysis (RSA) for a single seismic load case (LC). It summarizes, for eight computed vibration modes, the key modal quantities needed to combine individual modal contributions into an overall seismic demand. Below is a structured breakdown of its contents and how it ties back into the modal‐loading framework:

1. Table Layout  
   • Eight rows correspond to modes 1 through 8 (implicitly in ascending order).  
   • Five columns list, for each mode:  
     – q,max: Maximum modal coordinate response (in the chosen unit, here non‐dimensional) under the prescribed ground‐motion shape.  
     – f [Hz]: Natural frequency of the mode.  
     – ξ [%]: Modal damping ratio, expressed as a percentage of critical damping.  
     – T [sec]: Eigenperiod (T = 1/f).  
     – S(ξ,T): Pseudo‐acceleration spectral ordinate, normalized by peak ground acceleration.

2. Column Definitions (per provided context)  
   – q,max is the scalar maximum of the modal‐coordinate time history for that mode, obtained via the inner product of the mode shape and the seismic load pattern. It includes exact phase‐information (“Loading is exact including the phases”).  
   – f and T are reciprocals (T = 1/f) and characterise each mode’s dynamic “speed.”  
   – ξ is constant at 5 % for all modes, a common assumption in design spectra.  
   – S(ξ,T) is read directly from the design spectrum at the given period and damping.

3. Numerical Highlights  
   – Modes 1 and 6 (rows 1 and 6): q,max ≈ 6 ×10⁻¹⁶ and 8.6 ×10⁻¹⁷ – effectively zero participation, indicating these modes are not significantly excited by this seismic input.  
   – Modes 2 and 5: Highest responses (q,max ≈ 0.469 and 0.522), both at low frequency (0.565 Hz and 0.456 Hz), yielding large spectral values (S ≈ 0.565 g and 0.416 g).  
   – Modes 3, 4, 7, 8 cluster at f = 1.160 Hz (T = 0.862 s, S = 1.160 g), with intermediate q,max values alternating between ≈ 0.0103 and ≈ 0.2969.  
   – The three distinct frequency groups reflect the structure’s modal “families” (long‐period bending vs. shorter‐period modes).

4. Post-Processing Note  
   • As indicated beneath the table, subsequent combination of these modal responses will be carried out using the Square-Root-of-Sum-of-Squares (SRSS) or similar methods (“…iterations will be added as sum of squares.”).  
   • The modal response table is prepared so that each q,max can be weighted by factors (o–p) or squared eigenvector sums (2–p) if partial‐structure patterns are required in later steps.

In summary, Table 4.4 concisely presents all per‐mode dynamic properties and their seismic amplitudes, ready for SRSS combination, and reflects the uniform 5 % damping assumption as well as an exact phase‐inclusive loading.

The table reproduced above (Table 4.5: “Modal Responses – MTHA”) is the post‐processing output of a modal superposition calculation for the load case labeled “MTHA.”  In the workflow described, each load case is first decomposed into a set of loading functions (also called load patterns), then generalized loads (the scalar products of each eigenvector with each load shape) are computed, and finally the modal coordinate responses are assembled and combined.  Table 4.5 shows, for each mode retained in the analysis, the maximum absolute value of its modal coordinate q(t) over the time history of the multi‐harmonic response.  

Key features of the table:

  • Title: “Modal Responses – MTHA”  
  • Columns (repeated three times to economize space):  
      – Mode: the eigenmode number (©–p in the notation)  
      – q(t),max: the peak value of the modal coordinate for that mode under the given loading (in the same units as the generalized loads)  
  • Modes listed: 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18, 20 (mode 1 and other higher modes either have negligible response or were not retained)  
  • q(t),max values range over many decades:  
      – Some modes carry almost no dynamic contribution (e.g.Modes 2 or 17 have q(t),max on the order of 10⁻¹⁸)  
      – One or two modes dominate (Mode 5 reaches nearly 9.24×10⁻¹, Mode 8 about 3.10×10⁻², Mode 15 about 1.96×10⁻³)  
      – Remaining active modes exhibit intermediate values or very small contributions (10⁻³ to 10⁻¹⁸).  

Why this matters:  
  – In modal superposition, the total structural response is reconstructed by summing each mode’s contribution, typically via a root‐sum‐of‐squares (RSS) or direct combination.  Modes whose q(t),max falls below a truncation threshold can often be neglected without significant loss of accuracy.  
  – The dominance of a small number of modes (here, for example, mode 5) may indicate that the structure’s dynamic behavior under the MTHA load case is governed by certain natural frequencies.  
  – Knowing q(t),max per mode is the first step toward computing physical displacements, stresses, or forces by multiplying each q(t) by its corresponding mode shape.  

How it fits in the overall RAG/vector‐store context:  
  1. A preceding table would have listed all loading functions (e.g. harmonic loads, static forces, special load patterns).  
  2. Next comes a table of generalized loads: <X(o+p)> (sum of squares of modal values), 2 <X(62-p)>, etc., giving the modal participation factors and the square‐integrated loads.  
  3. Then this table (4.5) presents the maximum modal coordinate responses, q,max, for each mode in that load case.  
  4. Subsequent tables (not shown here) would typically include:  
     • Eigenfrequency f [Hz]  
     • Damping ratio ξ [%]  
     • Period T [s]  
     • Pseudo‐acceleration spectral response S(ξ,T), normalized to ground acceleration  

Taken together, these data allow the engineer to (a) identify which modes carry significant energy, (b) perform modal truncation sensibly, (c) compute mode‐by‐mode contributions to responses of interest, and (d) carry out spectral combination or time‐history reconstruction as required.

The table of functions and loads is always introduced before the description of the function, followed by the loads of this load case.
 The generalised loads of the individual modes and the sum of their squares are output in the case of a modal loading.

The displacements of the individual load cases are output by static analysis.
 In case of dynamic analysis the maximum displacements, velocities and accelerations can be output for all nodes. There result two lines per node with the minimum and maximum values as well as the corresponding time values if a time analysis was carried out. In case of stochastic or steady-state excitation the extreme values were computed by statistical methods or by analysis of one period of the steady-state excitation.
 Witha definition of ECHO DISP nn the print may be limited to those important nodes with a number less than the value nn.

The table presented (Table 4.6: Sum of forces (Base-Shear) (ECHO RESP)) summarizes the computed base shears (Vb) and base overturning moments (Mb) for a building model under dynamic excitation, combining two principal mode families via the SRSS (square‐root‐of‐sum‐of‐squares) rule. All values refer to the base of the structure (height H = 0 m) and represent extreme envelope results extracted from the time‐history or spectral response (“ECHO RESP”) analysis. No vertical (Z-direction) excitation is present, so Z-direction shears are zero in the mode‐by‐mode rows but a nonzero torsional moment (Z-moment) appears when the two modes are combined.

Column definitions  
• H [m]  
 – Elevation at which base shear is evaluated (here H = 0 m, i.e., the structure’s base).  
• Mode  
 – Identifier for the combination rule/axis. Both individual rows are labeled “SRSS²,” indicating SRSS combination at the squared‐sum stage for each orthogonal mode.  
• Vb X, Y, Z [kN]  
 – Base shear in global X-, Y- and Z-directions for the given mode or combined result.  
• Mb X, Y, Z [kNm]  
 – Overturning moment about global X-, Y- and Z-axes, computed with respect to the global origin, for the given mode or combined result.

Row-by-row interpretation  
1. SRSS mode A (predominantly X-direction)  
 • Vb: 49.5 kN in X, 2.3 kN in Y, 0.0 kN in Z.  
 • Mb: 17.49 kNm about X, 367.36 kNm about Y, 0.00 kNm about Z.  
 • Interpretation: The first principal mode produces large shear in X and an overturning moment about the transverse (Y) axis; a small orthogonal shear appears due to minor modal coupling.  
2. SRSS mode B (predominantly Y-direction)  
 • Vb: 2.3 kN in X, 48.6 kN in Y, 0.0 kN in Z.  
 • Mb: 363.02 kNm about X, 17.49 kNm about Y, 44.13 kNm about Z.  
 – Interpretation: The second principal mode yields large shear in Y and overturning moment about the X-axis, plus a modest torsional (Z-axis) moment from mode shape asymmetry.  
3. SRSS superposed total  
 • Vb: 49.6 kN in X, 48.7 kN in Y, 0.0 kN in Z.  
 • Mb: 363.44 kNm about X, 367.78 kNm about Y, 44.13 kNm about Z.  
 – Interpretation: Combined via SRSS, the two modes give nearly equal base shears in X and Y (reflecting symmetric stiffness/mass), zero vertical shear, and significant overturning in both orthogonal directions plus the torsional component from mode B.  

Contextual notes  
• These base forces/moments are the extreme values over all static or stochastic loading cases defined by the “ECHO RESP” analysis step.  
• For seismic or random vibration inputs, extremes may have been extracted statistically.
